collaboration/onboarding-share: Confirm Before Publishing
The rule that the agent must surface the share offer and wait for human approval before publishing.
Hosted-side Access Visibility Limit
The agent knows the tool's behavior but usually cannot see the hosted side's access scope or retention, so the human should verify org-side.
Onboarding Friction
The multi-step manual effort (clone, find, read, paste) required to transfer knowledge into a new teammate's agent when they are least oriented.
Onboarding Guide
A document in a repo describing its working model (source→build→release flow, feedback routing, where to file what), serving as the source of knowledge for new collaborators.
Onboarding Share
Publishing a repo's onboarding guide to a share link that a teammate's Claude Code agent can open directly, so the agent learns the working model in one click.
Optional Next Step Offer
Framing the share as a named, explained suggestion that the human decides whether to trigger, rather than a default action.
Outward Publish
Copying content to org-hosted infrastructure outside git, which is treated under the same bar as any external share.
Right Guide for Audience
Choosing between a client/engagement-specific guide and a scrubbed generic template according to who receives it.
Share Tool/Skill
The tool or skill that implements the mechanics of publishing a guide to a share link.
Snapshot Not Live Mirror
A published share link serves the content as of publishing; later edits don't propagate until the same link is re-published or updated.
Trust
Outward publishing rides on borrowed reputation, which is the origin of the confirm-first bar.
collaboration/teams: Avoiding silent stalling
Rule that a blocked teammate must immediately message the lead rather than stall silently.
Marking tasks completed
Updating task status via TaskUpdate when work is done, rather than only stating completion.
Merge conflicts
Conflicts arising when multiple teammates change shared files concurrently.
No git commits unless instructed
Rule that teammates should not commit to git unless their task explicitly says so.
Prefer Edit over Write
Guideline to use Edit instead of Write on shared files to reduce merge conflicts among teammates.
Progress reporting to lead
Using SendMessage to report progress, findings, and blockers to the team lead.
Read before editing
Guideline to read a file before editing since another teammate may have changed it.
Task list checking
Practice of checking the TaskList after completing each task to find the next work item.
Team lead
The coordinating agent to whom teammates report progress, findings, and blockers.
Teammate role
The role of an agent operating as a member of an agent team rather than as a solo agent.
data: The ongoing practices a database pulls in, such as migrations, schema docs, backups, and review, which constitute its real cost.
A data store (or graph extension) suited to densely interconnected, traversal-first data.
A lightweight storage option suited to ephemeral, single-process, small data.
Managed schema changes covering numbering, idempotency, and consolidation, needed once a server database is used.
A serverless, single-file relational database suited to local, single-writer data needing queries.
Generated schema reference and entity-relationship diagrams documenting a database.
Scoping the data layer to actual need
The principle of choosing data storage tooling proportional to the real requirements rather than habit.
A server-based relational database (Postgres/MySQL) managed with versioned migrations, for shared, evolving, multi-writer data.
Data that is shared among multiple writers and persists over time, justifying database discipline.
data/migrations: Checkpoint baseline consolidation
Consolidating a long migration history into a checkpoint baseline.
Database migration
A versioned change to a database schema or data, applied via a migration tool so that changes are tracked and reproducible.
Idempotent DDL
Re-runnable DDL that survives a retry.
Immutability of existing migrations
A rule that already-created migrations are never modified; changes are made by creating a new migration.
Irreversible migration
A migration, such as dropping a column or table, whose rollback cannot restore data.
Large table migration risk
The risk that a migration touching a likely-large table (users, events, logs) will cause problems, mitigated with online DDL or batching.
Migration explanatory comment
A comment in the migration explaining what it does and why.
Migration ledger and ordering
Numbering, ordering, and the applied-migrations ledger that tracks which migrations have been applied.
Migration naming convention and directory structure
The tool-specific conventions for naming migration files and organizing them in directories.
Migration tool detection
Identifying which migration tool a project uses (Prisma, Alembic, Knex, Flyway, ActiveRecord, raw SQL) so its conventions can be followed.
Mixing data and schema migrations
Combining data migration with schema migration in one migration, which is discouraged in favor of separation.
One logical change per migration
A practice of limiting each migration to a single logical change, such as not combining table creation with data transforms.
PR and CI delivery flow
The pull request and continuous integration process through which migrations land.
Rollback verification
Checking that running up then down leaves the schema unchanged, and flagging it if not.
Schema documentation regeneration
Regenerating schema docs and diagrams after a migration.
Up and down migrations
Paired create (up) and rollback (down) steps included in a migration so that changes can be applied and reversed.
data/migrations/checkpoint: Baseline faithfulness verification
Building a second throwaway database from the candidate baseline alone and diffing it against the replayed original to confirm they match exactly.
Checkpoint baseline consolidation
Consolidating a long migration history into a checkpoint baseline.
Checkpoint timestamp fingerprint
Consolidated versions share one applied-timestamp cluster for a checkpoint apply, versus spread timestamps for incremental replay, allowing the path a database took to be identified.
Generated baseline
A baseline produced by replaying the old baseline plus all migrations into a throwaway database and dumping the schema and seed data.
Graph/extension store catalog carry-over
Content a plain dump misses, such as an AGE label catalog, that must be carried into the baseline verbatim because it can't round-trip.
Hand-merging migrations
Manually combining migration files by eye into a baseline, which drifts from what the migrations actually produce.
Incremental replay
Applying migrations one by one over time, producing spread timestamps in the ledger.
Migration ledger and ordering
Numbering, ordering, and the applied-migrations ledger that tracks which migrations have been applied.
Retaining old migration files
Moving old migration files to an archive location rather than deleting them, since databases created before the checkpoint still need them.
Throwaway database
A temporary database used to replay migrations or build from a candidate baseline for dumping and comparison.
data/migrations/idempotent: Verifying a migration by running it, then running it again against the same database; the second run must produce no error and no change.
Protecting each DDL statement with existence guards so that re-running it does not error on already-existing objects.
The ability to recover from a migration that failed partway or was retried, rather than leaving the database wedged.
Record version last in same transaction
Inserting the applied-version ledger row as the final statement inside the same transaction as the migration changes, so failure leaves no row and the migration retries cleanly.
data/migrations/numbering: Consolidating a long migration history into a checkpoint baseline.
Unused or dropped numbers leave gaps that readers skip; gaps should not be backfilled or renumbered.
Re-runnable DDL that survives a retry.
Numbering, ordering, and the applied-migrations ledger that tracks which migrations have been applied.
A migration's number serves as its identity, and downstream databases record it once applied, so it must not be disturbed.
Two branches adding the same migration number collide, and must be resolved before merge by renumbering the not-yet-landed migration to the next free number.
New migrations take the next number in sequence; existing numbers are never renumbered or reused.
A naming scheme using timestamps as prefixes that avoids collisions at the cost of readability, suited to large or busy teams.
Filenames are zero-padded so lexical order matches numeric order, while code compares numbers as integers by stripping leading zeros.
data/schema-docs: A portable intermediate format that renders to interactive ER diagrams and pastes into dbdiagram.io.
The DDL defines the schema authoritatively, so documentation should be derived from it rather than transcribed from memory.
Grouping and packing tables in large diagrams
Color or group tables by logical schema and pack disconnected tables to keep large diagram layouts compact.
Schema documentation written manually becomes outdated as soon as a migration changes the schema.
A plain-text diagram format such as Mermaid kept for places where interactive viewers don't render, like a repo file browser.
Generated docs emit a reference (tables, columns, types, constraints, comments) and a diagram, serving different readers.
Wiring generation into the docs build so the page and diagram are rebuilt from the current schema each deploy.
Textual DDL parsing without live database
A generator reads DDL files directly instead of connecting to a database, so it runs in CI with only the interpreter, deterministically and without credentials.
documentation: Craft altitude
The group of child ways concerned with authoring a single artifact well, such as README, REST reference, code docs, diagrams, standards and validation.
Decision record (ADR)
A node type in the documentation graph representing an architecture decision, such as ADR-302.
Diátaxis classification
A classification enum based on reader posture (tutorial, how-to, reference, explanation).
Documentation as typed graph
A model in which each documentation page and decision record is a node and references are edges, forming one typed graph rather than a collection of files.
Filesystem as serialization
The filesystem, with its folders, names and rendered site, is a human-readable serialization and view of the graph, not the source of truth.
Invariant earns its place by real defect
Principle that an invariant is justified only if its violation is a genuine defect, such as a dangling edge, supersede cycle, or id/mode mismatch.
Linter
A tool that enforces node types and structural invariants across the documentation graph.
Model altitude
The group of child ways that type the corpus: the graph, typed node, classification enum, node types, type-checker and projection.
Node type in frontmatter
The type of each node is declared in frontmatter and enforced by a linter, rather than being encoded in the filename.
Progressive disclosure, task-orientation, currency
Principle of giving overview before detail, organizing by reader job, and keeping pages current, since an outdated page is a broken front door.
README as front door
The README serves as the front door of documentation.
Type once, serialize many
Principle that there is one typed graph with many views such as dev tree, published site, Obsidian graph and audience bundles; audience drives the view, not the type.
Validation by fresh agent
A cold read by a fresh agent given only the entry point grades the docs, with wrong answers treated as docs defects; linters are proven by a planted violation.
documentation/adr: Alternatives section
ADR section listing rejected options, with a concrete reason each lost; fullest for one-way decisions.
As-built observation exclusion
A detail reconstructed from source with no recorded rationale is not an ADR and belongs in an evidence record, design note or README marked 'rationale not recorded'.
Context section motivating example
Discovery that surfaced the need is relegated to one or two sentences in the Context section.
Deliberate deviation ADR
An ADR documenting an intentional departure from a standard, naming the standard, reason, scope and end condition so it is not mistaken for drift.
Doing nothing as a decision
Deferring action counts as a decision when alternatives were live; the ADR records the destination, the trigger for starting work, and why waiting is safe.
Generalize the decision
Practice of recording the durable, reusable principle in an ADR while excluding the discovery path and session-specific details.
Permanent ADR number
A record's number is permanent; layout-changing commands rewrite paths but leave citations as they are.
Project-specific ADR commands, format and lifecycle
The project's ADR commands, record format and lifecycle depend on the vendored tool and the contract it declares, and take precedence over habits from other projects.
Reversibility grade
A tag on every ADR classifying reversal cost as reversible, expensive or one-way, which may graduate at a known point.
Trip report anti-pattern
An ADR that only makes sense when one knows the story of the session that produced it, accreting exploration specifics instead of a reusable principle.
When to write an ADR
Criteria for deciding that a decision merits an ADR: architectural choices, trade-off approaches, process changes, security/performance decisions, and anything whose rationale must be remembered.
documentation/adr-context: ADR Discovery
The process of locating relevant ADRs, using the ADR tool if installed and querying rather than browsing.
Accepted Status Prioritization
Prioritizing ADRs with accepted status because they represent active decisions.
Agent Decision Records (ADR)
Project records documenting decisions that inform implementation work, with statuses such as accepted and a Summary section.
Context Consumption
Reading excessive material uses up the agent's context window without proportional benefit.
Decision Record Summary
A section of a decision record stating what was decided, what it trades away, and whether it is one-way, to be read before the body.
Evidence Records
Findings, surveys, and audits that serve as background cited by a decision and are read when the decision points to them.
Selective Reading Strategy
Reading only 1-3 most relevant records rather than the entire ADR corpus, to avoid wasting context.
Superseding Links
Links on a record pointing to the current version of a decision, which should be followed.
When to Check ADRs
Situations in which consulting ADRs is warranted, such as starting work in an area with likely decisions or risking contradiction of existing ones.
When to Skip ADRs
Situations in which reading ADRs is unnecessary, such as simple bug fixes, full user-provided context, or ADRs already read.
adr/v0
Project ADR version without an ADR tool, where record files are checked directly.
adr/v1
Project ADR version in which an ADR tool is available and records are queried rather than browsed.
documentation/adr/consider: Advisor
A second model or subagent given the goal condition or operator's words and asked whether a decision serves that intent; its answer is recorded attributed to the advisor.
Agent owns technical calls
The agent makes technical decisions and grounds each in evidence, a standard, upstream, or a precedent; the operator is never asked to approve them.
Approval before probes asked
If the operator approves before probes are asked, record their words without probe names, act, and put probes in the same reply without waiting.
Asking in plain words
Questions to the operator use plain language with enough context to answer without opening the file, rather than field names.
Canary
A deliberately wrong, harmless, never safety-related intent check asked only in conversation, used as a signal probe and never recorded in the record's text.
Consider step
The step in the decision workflow that records the operator's intent about a decision, while the agent owns the technical calls.
Decision Summary
An opening summary a reader can judge alone: what is decided, trade-offs and foreclosures, one-way status, probes, and an inversion.
Intent probes
Short intent checks, at most one or two, phrased in the operator's terms and answerable in a word, labeled by confidence in having read intent correctly.
Inversion
A statement naming the two ends the decision sits between; put to the operator only when it turns on what they want.
Missed canary
A canary that an answerer fails to catch; it is treated as information, noted once, and not chased.
Raising a concern
The agent may raise few, actionable concerns at any stage; challenged once, then proceeds; recorded as an entry that is answered or withdrawn, never deleted.
Recording operator answers
Answers are recorded as entries for probes the words settled; minimal or no answers are recorded as said, later answers are appended, and a 'no' is corrected by superseding or new record.
Reviewing past decisions
A process where the operator reviews decisions from recent sessions, walking through each from its Summary and recording reactions in the operator's name.
Showing evidence to operator
Where decisions carry evidence entries, show them by running the command, showing output, or opening the page, and state what was shown.
Unattended run
A run with no human present where the goal condition serves as the operator's stated intent basis for the consider step.
documentation/adr/migration: Bringing config to the records' contract
Step that adds the contract line and capabilities blocks to config when it declares an older contract, leaving other lines and comments untouched.
CI regression prevention
Using a non-zero exit code from a validation command in continuous integration to block regressions.
Capabilities from domains
Seeding one capability per v0 domain using the domain's description, then refining by keeping, splitting, renaming, or deleting each seed.
Case study: knowledge-graph-system capabilities
Example where 9 domains became 18 capabilities, and agent-ways went from 6 domains to 13 capabilities.
Converting existing records
A multi-step workflow of preparing files, scanning into import sheets, editing, dry-running, and applying to bring existing records into adr/v1.
Cross-reference updating
After moving files, searching for and fixing broken references to them.
Domain range design
Guidance to use 100-wide non-overlapping ranges, reserving 1-99 for legacy, with the tool assigning the next available number within a domain's range.
Dry-run apply
An apply mode that writes records into the corpus, lints them, prints issues, then restores every file and keeps the sheets.
Foreign ADR formats
ADR formats from other tools such as adr-tools, MADR, and Log4brains, for which no reader exists yet.
Greenfield setup
Scaffolding the full ADR structure for a project with no existing records, starting by vendoring the tooling and verifying.
Import sheets
Editable per-record files written by the scan step, containing open todo items for v1 fields the scan could not infer; apply skips sheets with open items.
Migration starting states
A classification of an existing project's ADR situation (greenfield, flat directory, v0 frontmatter, inline metadata, other tools), each with a matching migration strategy.
Multiple capabilities per record
A record may carry 2–3 capabilities when it changes several (ADR-308).
Numbers are permanent identity
Principle (ADR-310) that a record's number is its permanent identity; conversion never renumbers or re-homes a record by domain range, and ranges only allocate numbers for new records.
Operator-approved vocabulary refinement
Process of reading records, grouping by what decisions change, proposing capabilities to the operator with descriptions and examples, and applying only what the operator accepts.
Parking as legacy
Keeping a corpus not worth converting as read-only history in a legacy location, with a reserved range covering its numbers.
Post-migration validation
Verification step run after any migration to confirm the result is correct, using a command that exits non-zero on errors.
Preparing files the scanner can't read
Renaming sequential files to ADR-NNN names (keeping the number) and moving inline metadata into YAML frontmatter so the scanner can read them.
Thin vocabulary notice
A tool notice printed when at least 40 records sit under 2 or fewer domains/capabilities, or one domain holds 60% or one capability 50% of records, indicating coarse seeds.
Vendoring the tooling
Installing the ADR tooling by copying (not symlinking) it into the repo, as documented in the adr skill.
adr.yaml config
The config file defining a project's ADR structure, including domain range design and directories.
documentation/api: 404 on nested resources
Returning 404 when a parent resource in a nested route does not exist, rather than returning an empty list.
Common Claude Omissions
A checklist of API design practices that an AI assistant tends to forget when building API endpoints.
HTTP method semantics
PUT replaces, PATCH updates, and DELETE is idempotent.
HTTP status code conventions
Use 201 for creation, 204 for deletion, and 409 for conflicts.
Input validation
Validating the request body before processing and returning a 400 response with specific field-level errors rather than a generic message.
Pagination on every list endpoint
Practice of adding pagination to all list-returning endpoints from the start, because retrofitting it later is painful.
Per-project default API conventions
A set of default REST API conventions that can be overridden on a per-project basis.
Plural nouns for resources
Convention of naming REST resource collections with plural nouns rather than singular.
Retrofitting cost
Adding a feature such as pagination after the fact is more difficult than including it initially.
URL versioning
Convention of including the API version in the URL path.
documentation/diataxis: Closed 2×2 of documentation modes
A matrix placing every page by two questions: studying vs working, and practical steps vs theoretical knowledge, yielding four modes.
Explanation
An understanding-oriented page illuminating why something works as it does, design rationale, trade-offs and the bigger picture; studying + theoretical knowledge.
How-to
A task-oriented recipe for achieving a specific goal for someone who knows the basics; working + practical steps.
Mode as promise to reader
The mode signals to the reader what kind of help they are getting, and the page must stay faithful to its quadrant or be reclassified or split.
Mode choice as human judgment
Choosing the mode is the one decision the tool cannot make; the tool computes the id and writes frontmatter after the author decides the mode.
Mode drift failure
Classic failure where a tutorial keeps stopping to explain or a reference is padded with how-to steps.
No fifth mode
Rule that the four modes are closed; a page that won't fit one quadrant is two pages.
One mode per page
Rule that each page is exactly one of the four modes; mixing modes causes each to interrupt the other's job, so such pages should be split and cross-linked.
Reference
An information-oriented description of the machinery (APIs, flags, schemas, options); accurate, complete, consulted rather than read; working + theoretical knowledge.
Tutorial
A guided, learning-oriented lesson that takes a newcomer through doing something successfully; studying + practical steps.
documentation/docstrings: Docstrings are not needed for trivial getters, one-line helpers, or self-evident code.
A convention to use docstrings in every language, following each language's idiomatic documentation style.
Internal code whose intent is not obvious from its name should be documented with docstrings.
Public APIs, exported functions, classes, and modules should always have docstrings.
Each programming language has its own idiomatic documentation format, such as Google-style docstrings for Python or JSDoc for JavaScript/TypeScript.
documentation/markdown: Clause boundary vs mid-phrase test
A judgment test distinguishing authored one-clause-per-line prose (breaks at clause boundaries, varied lengths) from hard wrapping (mid-phrase breaks, uniform lengths).
Diff review after repair
Reviewing the diff after flattening is needed because the structural check cannot detect erased authored line breaks or non-CommonMark syntax.
Exact-string replacement edit failures
Edits that use exact-string matching must reproduce interior line breaks of wrapped paragraphs, causing misses and retries.
Hard wrapping
Inserting line breaks inside paragraphs at a fixed column width, regardless of phrase or clause boundaries.
Machine-ergonomics convention
A convention justified by costs to automated editing and review tools rather than by stylistic preference.
Non-markdown text formats exception
Formats without a reflowing renderer, such as plain text, commit bodies, and code comments, keep their wrapping conventions.
Non-semantic diffs
Reflowing a wrapped paragraph after a small change produces diffs showing many changed lines for one changed thought.
One line per paragraph convention
A markdown convention of writing each paragraph, list item, table row, and blockquote line on a single line rather than hard-wrapping to a column.
Structural line breaks
Line breaks that carry structure (list items, table rows, headings, blockquote labels, deliberate hard breaks, parallel clause-per-line prose) and should be preserved.
Structural reparse verification
Before writing, the repair tool reparses the result and compares document structure to the original, refusing to write on discrepancies.
Wide content allowed
Tables, long links, code lines, and fenced blocks may exceed comfortable reading width and should not be reflowed.
Wrap repair tooling
A pair of tools that detect hard-wrapped paragraphs (exiting non-zero) and flatten them with a backup, repairing only the enclosing paragraph and verifying structure by reparsing.
documentation/markdown/density: Cutting is cheap while text is in context
Text just written is still in context, so cutting is cheap, whereas the cost rises as time passes.
An automated check that counts decoration patterns in text an agent just wrote and reports the counts so the agent can cut them.
The frequency of em-dashes in prose; not wrong individually but a stylistic tic at high volume. It is counted, not banned.
The remedy of searching for flagged patterns and deleting them, since the surrounding sentence survives intact.
Tables, quoted passages, or documents about these patterns can score high legitimately; the agent may state this and move on, and the check will not fire again that session.
A sibling check concerning hard-wrapped prose in markdown documentation.
Reviewed prose in the repo has about 0.5 significance clauses per thousand words, while fresh drafts run several times that.
After cutting, the agent rereads and removes anything added back merely to preserve rhythm.
Clauses whose function is to tell the reader that the previous clause mattered, rather than adding information.
documentation/markdown/reflow: Cheap to fix now, costlier later
Text just written is still in context, so repairing wrapping immediately costs less than repairing it later.
The wrap detector is a heuristic that cannot distinguish column wrapping from deliberate one-clause-per-line prose.
False positive flag on already-fixed file
A repeated reflow flag on a file already reviewed is more likely a detector false positive than a missed repair, because the detector is a heuristic.
Preferred repair path in which the author rewrites the hard-wrapped paragraph flat as an ordinary edit, using the text already in context and judging whether breaks were mechanical or meant.
A permitted prose style where parallel clauses are deliberately broken onto separate lines, which is not column wrapping.
The 'ways author reflow --fix <file>' tool that backs up the original, repairs only detected paragraphs, reparses and compares, and writes nothing if anything beyond line breaks changed.
Wrapped paragraphs make later edits reproduce interior line breaks exactly and turn a small change into a multi-line diff.
documentation/mermaid: Matching the content (sequences, states, decisions, relationships, timelines, git) to the appropriate Mermaid diagram type rather than defaulting to flowchart.
Mapping color families to semantic roles and keeping one hue per role consistently across all nodes and diagrams.
The common mistake of using flowchart for all content, even when it has a time axis or state transitions.
Handling GitHub's Mermaid renderer quirks, such as line breaks in node labels, escaping angle brackets, and avoiding brackets in sequence messages.
Guidance to use Mermaid diagrams rather than ASCII art because Mermaid is diffable, renderable, and easy to edit.
Mid-tone subgraph strokes with translucent fill
Subgraph titles and borders land on the page, so they use mid-tone colors clearing ~3:1 contrast on both backgrounds, with translucent container fills.
Opaque node fills with per-fill text color
Using fully opaque node fills and choosing text color by fill brightness (dark on bright, white on deep) so contrast is theme-independent.
Styling for both light and dark themes
Choosing diagram colors so they remain legible against both white and near-black GitHub page backgrounds.
Rendering the diagram to confirm syntax parses and checking it in both light and dark previews.
documentation/readme: A documentation principle that a reader should understand what the project is and why it exists within 30 seconds.
A documentation anti-pattern of burying the 'what' of the project under 'how to install' instructions.
A documentation anti-pattern in which everything is placed in one massive file.
A documentation anti-pattern of assuming the reader already knows what problem the project solves.
A documentation anti-pattern of producing excessive documentation for trivial projects, such as 500 lines for a utility script.
A principle that documentation volume and structure should match project complexity: simple projects get a simple README, complex ones get a README plus docs tree.
A guideline mapping project complexity (script, library, application, platform) to the appropriate documentation set.
The organization of a docs/ directory, used when project complexity requires it.
documentation/standards: Practice of structuring standards as actionable rules rather than aspirational prose, kept short enough to be read and followed.
Automated continuous integration checks used to enforce coverage thresholds.
A table of typical standards domains (coding style, testing philosophy, dependency policy, accessibility, documentation) and what each covers or excludes.
Distinction that the Standards Way establishes standards while enforcement is delegated to tooling such as linters, CI checks, and review checklists.
A guidance area that measures adherence to standards through quality metrics.
Checklists used to enforce process compliance during review.
A guidance area about establishing and documenting the norms that define how a team works.
Practices to avoid: standards without rationale, standards duplicating tooling, and aspirational standards no one plans to enforce.
Situations when standards come up: starting projects, onboarding, policy decisions, and resolving style disagreements.
documentation/validate: Accepted false premise defect
The agent confirmed something the system does not do; fix by stating what the system does use on the first page a reader opens.
Author blind spot in self-review
Authors fill gaps in their own documentation from memory when rereading, so the page passes review while a newcomer stalls.
Documentation checks (linter, link checker, drift check)
Automated checks on documentation such as a docs linter, link checker, or drift check against generated pages.
Documentation defect classes
A table of defect types — wrong answer, source-only answer, accepted false premise, stale path — each with a corresponding fix.
False-premise question
A question asserting something the system does not do or use; a working page lets the reader reject the premise with a citation.
Fresh agent with only the entry point
A newly spawned general-purpose or Explore agent given only the entry point (README, index, onboarding guide) and none of the tested facts, used to validate documentation.
Grade against ground truth
Each wrong answer from the validation agent is treated as a defect in the documentation.
Load declaration
A requirement that the agent list what it read, in what order, and what it skipped before each answer; reaching the right answer by reading half the repository is a navigation failure.
Never use a fork for validation
A forked agent inherits the author's context and will pass a page that a stranger would fail, so validation must use a new agent.
Newcomer questions with known answers
Three to five questions such as how to run it, where X lives, what happens when Y, what to check before changing Z, whose answers the author already knows.
Planted violation test for checks
A check that has only reported green is untested; plant a violation, confirm it goes red with the right message, remove it, confirm green.
Re-run with same questions after fixes
After fixing docs, validation is repeated with the same questions, ideally graded by someone other than the author, with disclosure if unavailable.
Read-only agent
The validation agent is kept read-only so its report serves as evidence to act on.
Source-only answer defect
The agent had to read code to answer; fix by writing the missing section at the depth of the entry point.
Stale path defect
A link, command, or filename the agent followed did not deliver; fix by updating the reference and adding the case to the link check.
Wrong answer defect
The agent answered confidently and incorrectly; fix by correcting the cited passage or adding the needed one.
ea: Account iteration
The practice of scanning all configured accounts for a relevant platform, adapting to different tools, grouping results by account, and cross-referencing findings.
Autonomy with guardrails
A principle that the assistant gathers data, makes reasonable inferences and keeps moving, but asks a quick question when ambiguity or low confidence would meaningfully change output.
Email drafts
Email drafts created for user review instead of sending email directly.
Executive Assistant
An intelligent assistant that operates across multiple accounts and platforms to triage email, manage calendars, draft communications, track action items, and cross-reference data.
Explicit user approval
Required confirmation from the user before any mutation such as sending, creating or deleting.
Read-only by default
A principle that triage, review and intelligence workflows are read operations, while mutations require explicit user approval.
Safety rules
A set of per-action rules governing sending email or chat, deleting events, modifying files, and creating or updating tasks, time logs and invoices, requiring review or confirmation.
Silence is no
A rule that if the user ignores a suggestion, it is not re-suggested in the same session.
Suggest, never auto-execute
A principle that the assistant drafts, proposes and recommends changes, then waits for user confirmation before any write operation.
Trust model
The meta-level model that governs EA operations.
ea/briefing: The skill containing the runnable procedure for briefings: parallel scouts, priority structure, and suggested task mutations.
A unified briefing across inboxes, calendar, tasks, and chat that synthesizes what deserves the user's attention now.
Producing a cross-referenced picture of what needs attention across sources rather than dumping each inbox.
The cost of coordinating a team of subagents, which exceeds its benefit for simple or single-source tasks.
Using parallel scout subagents to gather briefing data across multiple accounts and services, hiding slow I/O and keeping raw fetches out of the lead's context.
Suggested changes to tasks, included in a briefing, which the user approves, modifies, or dismisses.
A lighter, direct approach for a single account or service, interactive task, or quick lookup where team orchestration overhead is not worth it.
Principle that a briefing ends in suggestions (ranked action list, proposed task mutations) and never sends, schedules, or mutates on its own.
ea/calendar: Calendar Management
The practice of creating, checking, and managing calendar events across multiple accounts.
Check availability before creating events
A workflow step requiring conflict queries across all relevant accounts for the proposed time range before an event is created.
Cross-account awareness
Checking all accounts for conflicts when scheduling, since personal events may block professional availability and vice versa.
Default local timezone
Defaulting to the user's local timezone unless otherwise specified, and always including timezone in event creation.
Explicit user approval
Required confirmation from the user before any mutation such as sending, creating or deleting.
Layered reminders for deadlines
Setting multiple reminders for important deadlines: 1 week before, 1 day before, and the morning of if applicable.
Post-meeting task capture suggestion
After a meeting is created or ends, asking whether action items should be captured as tasks.
Present event details before creating
Confirming event summary, start/end with timezone, description, attendees, and reminders with the user before creating the event.
Suggest, never auto-execute
A principle that the assistant drafts, proposes and recommends changes, then waits for user confirmation before any write operation.
Surface related tasks
When reviewing upcoming events, matching open tasks by client, project, or attendee names and informing the user.
ea/comms: Chat as context layer
Using a chat platform to enrich other workflows (meetings, email triage) rather than treating it as just another inbox.
Chat platforms
Human chat platforms such as Slack and Microsoft Teams accessed through their own tools for reading conversations and composing posts.
Chat triage
A process of scanning chat platforms: checking unread indicators across accounts, prioritizing 1:1 threads, noting meeting threads, and cross-referencing participants.
Cross-reference participants
Matching chat participants with email threads and calendar events.
Explicit user approval
Required confirmation from the user before any mutation such as sending, creating or deleting.
Meeting-related threads
Chat threads that carry pre-meeting context or post-meeting follow-ups, including shared links, files and action items.
Peer messaging between Claude sessions
A separate communication surface between Claude sessions, governed by its own rules, where replies need no approval.
Platform authentication
Browser-based chat sessions may expire; when redirected to login, the human is told and guided through re-authentication.
Posting requires approval
Posting anything to a chat platform requires explicit human approval after the draft is presented with target workspace and channel.
Prioritize 1:1 threads
Direct threads from real people are prioritized over group chats and channels.
Reading is safe
Reading chats, browsing channels, checking unread indicators and viewing history are always safe actions requiring no approval.
ea/comms/recap: A chapter-by-chapter AI-generated summary of a meeting with key discussion points.
Comparing AI summary action items with the task system to find tracked items, new obligations, and commitments by others.
Auto-extracted action items from a meeting, including assignees.
Structured post-meeting content such as summaries, transcripts, notes, mentions, recordings, and action items provided by meeting platforms.
Full speaker-attributed text of a meeting with timestamps, useful for understanding what was actually discussed.
For recurring meetings, pulling the previous occurrence's recap to establish what was discussed, assigned, and still open.
Other post-meeting content: shared notes, @-mentions, and video/audio recordings with playback controls.
Long transcripts may load incrementally, requiring scrolling or pagination to get complete content.
Searching within transcripts to find specific topics.
ea/email: Action Required section
Presentation section listing emails needing a response that the user has not replied to, ranked by urgency.
Already Addressed section
Presentation section listing messages with sent replies found in the thread, with a brief note of what was said.
Calendar cross-reference
Fetching calendar events for the same period to match meetings with related email threads.
Date range determination
Parsing relative time references such as 'last 24 hours' or 'since Monday' into concrete timestamps.
Email Drafting
The skill of composing draft email replies in the user's voice for review, without sending them directly.
Email Triage
A workflow that scans emails across all accounts for a time period, filters noise, cross-references with calendar and tasks, and presents a summary.
Filter-in criteria
Rules for keeping real people expecting responses, meeting-related threads, deadlines, invitations, and anything mentioning the user by name.
Include when uncertain
When uncertain whether an email is noise, include it with a note rather than filtering it out.
Noise filtering
Rules that exclude purchase receipts, shipping notifications, marketing, automated alerts, recruiting spam and subscription renewals, and report a brief count of what was excluded.
Open Tasks in Play
Presentation section listing tasks related to people, clients or topics surfaced in the triage.
Per-account inbox fetch
Retrieving messages for the period from each account's inbox, reading full content, extracting headers and noting thread IDs.
Response status check
Fetching sent messages for the same period to determine whether an inbox thread has a later sent reply, indicating the user already responded.
Sent Items of Note
Presentation section for outbound emails that may generate follow-ups.
Suggested Task Actions
Presentation section proposing Create, Complete, Update, or Stale? actions on tasks.
Triage suggestions
Presentation section with scheduling recommendations, deadline reminders, and follow-up nudges.
Voice and attribution
Guidance on voice and attribution in email, referenced as a related trust topic.
ea/email/drafting: Anti-patterns (AI tells)
Common AI-generated phrases and habits, such as stock pleasantries, corporate jargon, excessive hedging, and unnecessary numbered lists, that must be avoided in drafts.
Attachment handling
Fetching attachments from file storage and constructing a proper multipart message.
Create platform draft only after approval
Iteration rule: do not re-create the platform draft on each revision; create it once the user approves the final version.
Email Drafting
The skill of composing draft email replies in the user's voice for review, without sending them directly.
Email threading
Preserving the threading chain by extracting Message-ID, References and In-Reply-To headers so the draft is a reply in the correct thread.
Never send directly
Rule that emails must never be sent automatically; only drafts are created for user review.
Present for review and iterate
Workflow step of presenting the draft text to the user and revising it based on feedback.
Read original thread
Workflow step of reading the full original email thread to understand context before drafting.
Style Calibration
Process of matching drafts to the user's observed patterns in length, greeting/sign-off, contractions, tone and structure, using sent mail as the authority.
Writing style study
Reading 5-8 recent sent emails from the relevant account to calibrate tone, length, greeting, sign-off and vocabulary.
ea/intelligence: Chat history review
Checking the meeting's group chat for pre-meeting context and shared links.
Cross-Service Intelligence
Pulling data across email, calendar, file storage, chat, meeting recordings, and tasks to build a complete picture.
Meeting Prep
A workflow that gathers calendar details, emails, chat, prior meeting records, documents, and open tasks to prepare the user for a meeting.
Meeting continuity
For recurring meetings, pulling the previous occurrence's recap to establish what was discussed, assigned, and still open.
Open tasks surfacing
Surfacing commitments related to the meeting's attendees, client, or project.
Prep brief
A concise summary presenting who is attending, what has been discussed, what is open, and what to bring up.
Recent email threads with attendees
Email threads with meeting attendees reviewed to see what has been discussed recently.
Shared documents check
Checking file storage for recently shared or edited documents related to the meeting topic.
Stale task candidates
Tasks 14+ days old with no activity flagged for cleanup.
Suggested actions
Weekly review section recommending cleanup, follow-ups, and preparation for next week.
Surface related tasks
When reviewing upcoming events, matching open tasks by client, project, or attendee names and informing the user.
Task dashboard
Weekly review section with Eisenhower breakdown, completed vs. created tasks, and overdue items.
Time allocation
Weekly review section reporting hours by client or project.
Weekly Review
A comprehensive end-of-week synthesis across calendar, email, chat, files, and tasks.
Weekly review document synthesis
Synthesizing the weekly review into a document only if the user requests it.
ea/tasks: Cross-referencing action items with tasks
Comparing AI summary action items with the task system to find tracked items, new obligations, and commitments by others.
Don't fabricate due dates
Rule to set a task due date only from content, and not invent one if none is mentioned.
Suggest, never auto-execute
A principle that the assistant drafts, proposes and recommends changes, then waits for user confirmation before any write operation.
Suggesting Task Cleanup
Identifying stale tasks during briefings and reviews using age, overdue, and project-inactivity triggers.
Suggesting Task Completion
Proposing that a task be marked done when signals indicate fulfillment, such as a sent email or passed event.
Suggesting Task Creation
Proposing new tasks when a workflow surfaces a new obligation, with populated title, source, priority, and due date.
Suggesting Task Updates
Proposing changes to task properties when intelligence indicates they should change, such as deadline changes or unblocking.
Task Lifecycle
Personal task management framework treating tasks as the persistence layer closest to the user's brain, tracking obligations, deadlines, and commitments.
Task cross-reference pattern
Pattern that every intelligence-gathering workflow should cross-reference its findings with tasks.
Task source traceability
Recording the source type and reference on a task so its origin can be traced.
ea/tasks/time: Client and project matching
Mapping each work item to a client and optionally a project.
Invoice pre-confirmation summary
Billing period, total hours, line items by project, and calculated amount presented before creating an invoice.
Invoicing
Creating invoices, which requires explicit confirmation after presenting billing period, total hours, line items by project, and calculated amount.
Log on approval only
Rule that time is never auto-logged; entries are logged only after user approval.
Logging Workflow
The process of mapping work items to clients/projects, proposing time entries, and logging only upon approval.
Propose time entries
Presenting a summary of proposed time entries to the user before logging.
Time Tracking & Billing
A skill for logging billable hours against clients and projects, with confirmation required before logging.
Uninvoiced time
Logged time that has not yet been billed and may need invoicing.
Utilization
Hours logged compared to calendar time.
Weekly Time Review
A weekly review of hours by client and project, comparison to a typical week, utilization, and uninvoiced time.
evaluative: Author role
The agent that writes the software under evaluation.
Cited count from a run in this change
A pass count cited in a commit, PR, or handoff must name the command and be produced after the last edit.
Gates and instruments proven
Skipped checks read as skipped and each instrument has been seen red once.
Harness exits nonzero on failure
A harness that prints failures but exits zero leaves the agent as the only gate; the run must fail when a check fails.
Harness grows with the product
Features ship their check in the same change, and escaped defects become cases before the fix lands.
Held-out data against naive baseline
Loop for predictive models of time-ordered data using held-out future data compared to a naive baseline.
Instruments
The harness, drivers and readouts that run the product and observe it.
Loop types by output

Different output types (interactive program, platform behaviour, installer, port, ranking, model answer, agent, predictive model, measurement, context change, test cases) are matched to loops with distinct judges.
Oracle
What the output is compared against: a frozen baseline, external reference, sample metric, rubric, or the operator.
Oracle changes are separate and shown to operator
A change to the oracle is its own change, shown to the operator with what moved and by how much.
Residual from model of normal behaviour
Judging measurements with no fixed expected value by a model of normal behaviour and its residual.
Unverified done claim trigger
The situation where a change is about to be called done based only on it reading correctly, looking right, or author confidence, with nothing outside the author having run it.
Verdict read back from an instrument
Done is defined as a verdict the agent read from an instrument, as opposed to one the agent asserted, which is merely a claim.
evaluative/ablation: Cost scaling
Cost scales as scenarios × arms × trials, so the loop is run locally and on demand rather than on every merge.
Deterministic end-state checks first
Grading weights deterministic end-state checks (file exists, command not run, test passes) before rubric dimensions, with 'unknown' allowed.
Impression of improvement without comparison
The situation where a change seems better based on a few conversations without comparison against the version without the change.
Independent blind judge
An independent model that grades both arms' results without being told which arm produced which, with order shuffled per scenario.
Isolated environment per arm
Running each arm in its own disposable environment, such as a container with its own credentials, so neither can read the other's leftovers.
Multiple trials per arm and scenario
Running several trials for each arm and scenario and reporting trial counts, model and version, and resources.
Positive control (engagement check)
Confirming in every treatment trial that the change actually engaged, e.g. guidance loaded, tool called, skill invoked.
Remove-one arms
Arms containing everything in the treatment except one piece, used to attribute the contribution of that piece in a bundled treatment.
Run-to-run noise baseline
The spread between two identical arms, measured by running the baseline against itself; differences smaller than it are not findings.
Treatment arm
The arm in which the agent runs with the change, with everything else identical to baseline.
evaluative/agent-eval: 0% pass rate indicates broken task
With frontier models, a 0% pass rate across many trials most often signals an ambiguous, impossible, or wrongly graded task rather than an incapable agent.
Agent-eval loop
An evaluative loop that scores whole runs of an agent (multi-turn, tool-calling, environment-changing) over many trials rather than single answers.
Capability suite
Tasks the agent cannot yet do reliably; low pass rates are expected.
Code graders
Deterministic graders that are reproducible and fast but brittle to valid variation; mitigated by numeric tolerance and format normalisation.
Grade the outcome and transcript
Grade what the agent produced in the environment rather than a fixed step sequence, and also check the transcript, including hard path checks where constraints apply.
Graders hard to game
Graders should require actually solving the task rather than exploiting a loophole, and be tested on both positive and negative cases.
Graduation and suite growth from real failures
Capability tasks passed reliably graduate to the regression suite, and suites grow from real failures including user-reported ones.
Human grading
Human grading is the reference for calibrating model graders but is too slow and costly for every trial.
Model graders
LLM-based graders used where judgement is needed, with a clear rubric, one dimension, reasoning before scoring, an 'unknown' option, partial credit, a different model, and calibration against humans.
Read the transcripts
Verify graders by reading transcripts and grades; fix grader faults in the grader and loopholes in the task or grader, reporting each fix as a judge change.
Record trial configuration
Recording the model, version, and resource configuration with each run, since differences under about 3 percentage points deserve skepticism until configurations are matched.
Reference solution for every task
A known working output passing all graders, proving the task is solvable and the graders accept a correct answer.
Regression suite
Tasks the agent already does, with pass rates near 100%; a drop is a defect.
Repeat trials and pass@k / pass^k
Run several trials per task; pass@k means at least one of k succeeds, pass^k means all k succeed and falls as k grows; report tasks and trials counts.
Task, trial, transcript, outcome, grader
Vocabulary: a task has defined inputs and success criteria; a trial is one attempt; the transcript records it; the outcome is the final environment state; graders score aspects of a trial.
Trial isolation and clean environment
Starting each trial from a clean environment to avoid correlated infrastructure failures and answer leaks from shared state.
evaluative/clean-room: Author-machine blind spot
Tests on the authoring machine run against a configured checkout with pre-existing tools, settings and leftovers, so installer, upgrade and first-run defects go unseen.
Branch flavour
Clean-room run using the checkout's committed state and freshly built binaries, answering whether this change installs.
Clean-Room Loop
A verification loop that installs the product from nothing into a fresh, disposable environment and uses it as a new user would, proving the install path.
Disposable environment
A fresh, throwaway environment starting from an empty machine used to run the install.
First-run exercise
After install, driving the product's entry points with real event payloads from the written configuration, asserting expected output and zero exit codes.
Fix earliest failing section first
Report each failure by name with installer output, and fix the earliest failing section first because later ones cascade from it.
Idempotent install (run it twice)
A dry-run twice prints identical output and reports nothing to do, and a second real run changes nothing.
Missing dependency kept missing
Leaving a dependency out of the image on purpose and asserting the install fetched the prebuilt artifact, rather than adding a toolchain to make a failing run pass.
Pinned base image and tool versions
Pinning the base image and every tool version in one place read by both image and runner, with date-keyed cache-bust for moving targets.
Release flavour
Clean-room run using the published artifact through the documented install command, answering whether what users download works today and catching drift.
Seeded user home directory
Seeding the home directory with a real user's configuration, hooks, plugins, settings and untouched directories, then asserting files survive, hooks run and untouched directories hash identically.
Slow, tiered run schedule
The room is slow, so it runs locally before release and on demand in CI, release flavour on schedule, with money-spending tiers opt-in atop a passing install tier.
Unprivileged install user
Running the install as an unprivileged user so bind-mounted artifacts are owned by the host user and cleanup needs no elevated rights.
evaluative/fidelity: Agent reads queue only
Only queued cases are opened and read, explained, and fixed or proposed as deltas; auto-passed cases stay unopened.
Cite held source or label guess
Every fidelity claim cites a held source or is labelled a guess, and anachronisms or convenience the original lacked are fenced and named.
Cross-check with a second implementation
Running multiple implementation paths over the same inputs and requiring agreement, so disagreement reveals a defect without an answer key.
Deltas approved by operator and recorded with size
A baseline moves only with operator approval against a change report, and each approved delta is recorded with its magnitude for lineage auditing.
External reference as answer key
An existing output such as a lost program's output, published table, measured trajectory or older implementation's results, used as the ground truth.
Fidelity instrument
Measurement of output against the external reference, stating numbers such as residuals and differences and what remains unexplained.
Fidelity loop
An evaluation loop where the target already exists elsewhere and an external reference serves as the answer key, using separate instruments for regression and fidelity.
Fix the model, not the symptom
A model wrong against the reference is fixed in the model; symptom patches that make one frame look right hide the fault and are removed once the model is fixed.
Gate output for long suite
Each gate prints a single pass/fail line, logs fully to disk, prints only failing lines on failure, allows slices while iterating, and runs in full before a change is proposed.
Image diff scoring with numerics
Auto-pass requires both a pixel score above threshold and identical numerics; any changed count or header value queues the case regardless of pixel score.
Port or rewrite applicability
The situation of porting, rewriting or replacing an old system where the new version must produce the same output as the old one, with only spot checks done.
Regression instrument (frozen baseline)
A byte-exact capture of the current approved output used to detect whether a change moved anything, without judging correctness.
evaluative/forecast: Forecast loop
An evaluative loop in which the agent writes a model predicting a time-ordered signal and is judged on later-in-time data it has not seen.
Freeze the test window first
The held-out period is chosen and recorded before fitting anything and is not moved, shortened or trimmed after seeing results.
In-sample fit is insufficient
A model scoring well only on training data or a past it has already seen gives unknown performance after the training period.
Leakage check

Verifying that future information has not entered training via whole-series features, scaling on all data, rolling statistics including the target period, or tuning on the test window; preprocessing is fitted inside each training fold.
Match model family to signal
Choosing a forecasting model family (ARIMA, Fourier, state-space, neural nets, reservoir computing, delay embedding) suited to the signal's structure, starting with the simplest.
Mean absolute scaled error per horizon
A scale-free error metric dividing forecast MAE by the in-sample MAE of a one-step naive forecast, reported per forecast horizon; below 1 beats naive.
Naive baseline
A simple forecast such as the last value, the value one season ago, or the mean, scored on the same backtest as the model.
Random split leaks the future
On time-ordered data a random train/test split places future observations in the training set.
Residual diagnostics
Checking that one-step-ahead residuals look like noise, with no autocorrelation, trend or periodic pattern, which would indicate missed structure.
Simplest family first
Start with the simplest family the signal allows; a more complex model must beat a simpler one on the same frozen backtest.
Walk-forward backtest
A rolling-origin evaluation that fits on data up to a cut-off, forecasts the next horizon, advances the cut-off and repeats, reporting errors across all origins.
evaluative/held-out: Author-shared assumptions in self-written cases
Cases the author writes share the author's assumptions and vocabulary, so a tuned subject learns to pass them.
Close gap with new self-written cases
A large gap is closed by changing the subject against new self-written cases and then scoring a fresh held-out set.
Echo of subject wording
A writer who has read the subject's wording writes cases that echo it, and those cases measure the echo rather than the subject.
Fresh agent as case writer
The held-out cases are written by an agent with no session context; a stronger model gives a stronger check, same tier is cheaper.
Held-out cases
Test cases written by someone who has not seen the subject, kept from the author during tuning and scored only at the gate.
Report both scores with counts
Report the held-out score beside the self-written score with case counts for each.
Retire seen cases
Once the author has seen a case's failure it becomes training data, so the set is retired and new cases are written for the next gate.
Same author writes code and all tests
The trigger situation where the same person or agent wrote the code and every test, and all pass, checking only what the author thought to check.
Score only at the gate
The held-out set is scored only at the gate; the author sees the score and count but not the failing cases.
Self-fit gap
The distance between the held-out score and the self-written score, measuring how far the author fit its own cases.
Situation-only writer brief
The writer sees one sentence stating the situation the subject serves, never the implementation, configuration, trigger words, or existing cases.
Spread of case types
Requested mix of plain cases, indirectly phrased cases that don't name the topic, and near-misses that should not match.
Store set apart with provenance
The held-out set is stored where the author does not read it during tuning, recording who wrote it, from what statement, and when.
evaluative/model-oracle: Enough repetitions to estimate spread
Multiple measurements per commit are needed to estimate spread honestly; a single timing puts machine noise into the reference window.
Flagged residual is a finding
A residual beyond the threshold must be investigated by rerunning, bisecting or explaining, not dismissed by widening the threshold or refitting including the new result.
Frozen reference window
A window of known-good behaviour (e.g. last N commits, a week of telemetry) on which the model is fitted and which is recorded.
Keep the measuring host still
Pin the host, build flags and input and record them with each run to reduce measurement noise.
Model-oracle loop
An evaluation loop where the oracle is a model of the system's normal behaviour fitted from its own history, and the residual between prediction and observation decides the verdict.
Multiple-series false alarm control
With many monitored series, k must be set for the whole family or false-discovery rate controlled, since per-series thresholds produce frequent false alarms.
Non-deterministic outputs with no fixed answer
Outputs such as latency, memory use, error rate or benchmark timing that vary run to run, so a fixed limit either fires on noise or misses real shifts.
Regime change is a baseline change
Refitting the model after a legitimate system change is a change to the oracle, requiring operator approval with old and new windows and shift size, never done silently.
Robust spread (MAD)
Centring on the median and scaling by median absolute deviation (times ~1.4826) or using percentile bands, to avoid outlier inflation of standard deviation.
Threshold set before the change
The residual threshold is derived from the residual's spread on the reference window and fixed before the change under test is measured.
evaluative/perceptual: A scenario per feature

Each feature adds a named scenario that drives to it, asserts on state, and contributes captures; names, debug keys and playtest list derive from one registry, and bugs become scenarios before the fix.
Agent as instrument
In the perceptual loop nothing can call the result right without someone reading the image, so the agent is itself one of the instruments.
Capture at multiple sizes
Capture screens at phone portrait, tablet, and desktop sizes, including titles, menus and overlays, since layout breaks at the edges.
Counters for countable behaviour
Adding counters (e.g. a bounce counter) to code so tests can assert on behaviour as numbers; the counters are part of the dev surface.
Drive real input
Send key and pointer events through the real browser or toolkit input path rather than calling movement functions directly.
Expose handles that set state
Provide dev hooks to jump to levels, force spawns, or grant invulnerability so scenarios reach cases directly instead of playing to them.
Expose state in development builds
Provide a global state handle (scene, score, position, dialog) in dev builds behind a dev flag so the harness can read it, preferring numbers over pixels.
Fixed sleep drift
Fixed sleeps drift because capture calls cost time and timers run differently headless, so screenshots may miss the intended animation.
Look and say what you saw
After a visible change, capture affected screens, read the images, describe each in a sentence, and compare to the expected result; fix and recapture if off.
Perceptual loop
An evaluative loop where an agent drives a running program headlessly, reads its state and screenshots, and looks at the output to judge visible changes.
Wait on state, never on time
Poll exposed state until a condition holds before acting or capturing, instead of using fixed sleeps that drift.
evaluative/probe-set: Adoption rule
A change is adopted when it gains on the changed path and loses nothing in separation, with untouched paths identical row-for-row.
Fitting data disjoint from evaluation sets
Data used to fit any tuned parameter must be disjoint from every evaluation set, and the data used must be named.
Grid sweep reporting all points
Sweeping a small grid of settings and reporting every point including losers, with a recommended default carrying a one-line reason.
Hand-checked examples insufficient
Trying a handful of examples by hand shows apparent improvement but cannot reveal whether other inputs got worse or false matches appeared.
Margin reporting
The margin below the decision threshold is reported, and a gain that spends most of the margin is reported as such.
Probe-set loop
An evaluation loop that scores a fixed set of cases before and after a change to a scoring, ranking, matching or routing mechanism, adopting the change only on the metric result.
Real inputs join the gate
When a store of real inputs exists, its results are added to the gate.
Results file record
Each evaluation is written to a results file with commands, corpus or build, table, surprises, and measured-but-not-adopted variants so questions are not reopened without new evidence.
Row-for-row diff of untouched paths
Paths the change should not touch must produce identical outputs, checked by diffing outputs rather than comparing totals.
Sampled set committed and reproducible
A set drawn by a rule (one case per category, a hash) and committed so every run scores the same rows, regenerated by the rule when the source changes and checked in CI.
Self-evaluated label
Because sets are authored by the system's builders, results show the system follows its authored structure and are labelled self-evaluated with row counts, not real-world quality.
Unrelated set (separation)
A set of inputs that should match nothing, used to measure separation: how far the strongest wrong score sits below the decision threshold.
Variants of the set
Set variants such as multi-part inputs or inputs with noise in front that reach other code paths.
evaluative/rubric: Calibrated model judge
A model used as a judge is calibrated before its verdicts count.
Check script must parse
The runner parses each check script before running it and fails the scenario if it does not parse, since a parse error stops checks partway while reporting a full pass.
Deterministic checks on run behaviour
Checks independent of phrasing, such as clean exit, expected context loaded, one commit made, clean working tree, or linter passing.
Known-good and known-bad answer testing
Each rubric item is tested against a known-good answer that should hit and a known-bad answer that should miss.
Model-written text non-determinism
Language model output such as summaries or release notes varies between runs, so exact-match tests fail every run and quality gets judged by reading a few outputs.
Quoting is part of the pattern
Characters the shell interprets inside a quoted pattern change what the pattern is, so single-quoted patterns are preferred.
Rubric items as patterns
Each rubric item is a pattern the answer should contain; a scenario passes when at least a stated number of items hit.
Rubric loop
An evaluative loop for model-written text that runs each scenario and judges the result with deterministic checks on what the run did plus a rubric on what the answer said.
Scenario
A fixed setup (project directory, seeded files, prompt, sometimes a second turn) plus a check script, run with the real model, tools and configuration.
Variance and cost handling

A single run is one sample; flipping scenarios are rerun several times and reported with hit rate and count, and live runs cost tokens so the suite runs when a change alters what the model sees or does.
evaluative/sandboxed: Bounded agent commands
Limiting the agent's own commands so they do not load the host, e.g. filesystem searches walking network mounts or render loops in a windowed nest.
Command channel into the subject
A route for sending commands to a subject lacking its own IPC, via something it reads such as a configuration key and sequence number, with verbs added as tests need them.
Ground truth by a separate route

Confirming the subject's effect via an independent source, such as the platform's scripting interface listing window geometry or a probe window logging presses; on disagreement the subject is wrong until shown otherwise.
Isolated nested or virtual platform instance
A nested or virtual instance of the real platform started with its own configuration, session bus, data and cache directories and a name, preferably using a virtual output.
Real input injection
Injecting pointer and key events through the platform's input protocol rather than calling the subject's handlers directly.
Recording nest-vs-real platform divergences
Recording known differences between the nest and the real platform where the next session will read them, and having build-dependent suites check the build and skip loudly on others.
Risk of running subject on live host
Loading a plugin or extension into the host one is working in risks breaking the operator's editor or session, and the platform hides most of what happens.
Sandboxed loop
An evaluation loop that runs a second, isolated instance of the real platform hosting the subject and builds a channel into it, so the operator's live session is not put at risk.
Subject's self-reported state
The subject's own state line reports what it believes, not necessarily what is true.
Tell for harm to the host
A platform-specific signal, such as a stall warning in the live journal or a reload of the live configuration, watched during every run to detect harm to the host.
Text state readout after every command
The subject writes its full state as one parseable line plus a line per object after every command, so tests can assert on numbers; screenshot comparison is a secondary instrument.
Verify isolation rather than assume it

Practice of listing what the nest touches on the host (file modification times, live platform log) and treating any change as a failure, since helper processes inherit environment variables pointing to the live session.
itops/incident: Contextual Escalation
Practice of providing the original request, diagnostic steps, evidence, hypotheses, and rationale when escalating an issue.
Data Restore as Last Resort
A data restore is a separate, separately approved last resort and should not be used to fix configuration problems.

meta/choices: Batch pending decisions
When multiple decisions are stacked up, put them through the tool together, one question each, rather than as a prose list.
Carry context in each question
Each question should state what was built or decided and what the answer changes, so the human can answer without opening artifacts.
Decide and state when one option is clearly right
When one option is clearly right, or a fact is verifiable yourself, pick it, say what and why, and proceed rather than asking.
Don't ask what you've been told
If the human has already decided, act on it rather than re-asking.
Genuine branch point
A set of distinct options whose answer changes what you do next.
Hedging question
Asking 'is my plan ready / should I proceed?' is not a real choice but hedging.
Keep choices small
Limit to two to four options per question and a handful of questions at most.
Lead with a recommendation
Place the option you would pick first and mark it, so the choice has a point of view.
Make options distinct with tradeoffs
Options should lead to genuinely different outcomes, and each should state its tradeoff along with its label.
Over-asking causes rubber-stamping
Asking about non-genuine forks trains the human to rubber-stamp, like a linter nagging on non-defects, defeating the point of asking.
Present genuine branch points as explicit choices
When a real fork with distinct options affects the next action, surface it as a structured explicit choice rather than burying it in prose or choosing silently.
Respecting human's time
A clean choice surface saves the human time versus prose walls or guessing and making them undo it.
Structured choice tool
A harness tool offering structured options with short headers, a recommended default, and one-line tradeoffs.
Vary interaction shape to the decision
Match the interaction to the decision's complexity: tool for simple, prose/doc flow or demonstrated work for complex, and vary it to avoid fatigue.
meta/compaction-checkpoint: Active goal across compaction
A session-scoped goal survives compaction, so the synthesis should restate the goal condition, keep the checkpoint light, and consider finishing nearly-done work first.
Ask the user for calibration
Step of presenting the summary and asking 1-2 focused questions to determine whether work is on track, needs adjustment, or pivoting, and which threads matter most.
Compaction checkpoint
A structured sync with the user performed near the context limit, before mandatory compaction, to produce a synthesis that survives compaction.
Continuance prompt
A short copy-pastable block with goal, what's landed, immediate next step, and key files/branches that lets the user resume in a fresh session after a hard reset.
Directed compaction
User-directed, synthesis-anchored compaction performed after writing the synthesis, as opposed to uncontrolled generic compaction.
GitHub issue persistence (ADR-180)
Synthesis is placed on a labeled GitHub issue when no task list exists, and issues behind the task list survive compaction.
Summarize where things stand
Step of giving a concrete, concise summary of goals, accomplishments, remaining work, decisions with rationale, and uncertainties.
Task list update with user input
If active tasks exist, their descriptions are updated with the user's input to carry state through compaction.
Uncontrolled compaction
Generic compaction where the system decides what to keep, without user steering or a synthesis anchor.
User continuous persistence
The user persists continuously across compaction and can therefore provide synthesis that survives it best.
Write the synthesis
Combining the summary and the user's steering into a checkpoint file, using task descriptions or a labeled GitHub issue, in the user's own words.
meta/deployment: Activation dry-run plan
A preview of activation showing each root as linked/link/relink/refused and the settings merge outcome, touching nothing; the answer when users ask whether agent-ways will touch their files.
Claude guiding adopters through install
Many adopters' first touch is the installer, with a Claude reading errors and guiding them, so Claude must avoid hazards like steering users into clobbering or drifting.
Establish legacy vs projection before giving command
The key decision is whether the install is a pre-1.0 in-place clone; if so, point to migration instead of updating or reconciling.
Fresh install
The installer one-liner stages the app, builds it, links binaries, and reconciles to materialize the projection and merge settings, preserving existing user config.
Legacy in-place clone
A pre-1.0 install topology where the config directory was itself the git clone of the app; it must be migrated rather than updated in place.
Migration
A gated, backed-up process that moves a legacy in-place install to the 1.0 projection model, performed by a migrator built from a tagged release.
Non-destructive preservation of user files
Install refuses to replace real directories or files at projected roots; it stops and names the path, or renames to a timestamped sibling, never deleting anything.
Per-project opt-out
A project can switch ways off for itself via a setting in its project config.
Repair
Reconcile alone re-materializes missing or stale projected roots, but stops on legacy in-place clones.
Targets (activation)

Targets are Claude Code config directories where the install is active; installation and activation are separate states, and reconcile converges enabled targets and withdraws from disabled ones (ADR-184).
Thin projection install model
In 1.0, the Claude config directory is a thin projection of an XDG application: symlinks to projected roots plus a settings merge, while the app itself stays in its XDG location.
Update via reprojection
Updating involves pulling app source or re-running the installer and then reconciling; because roots are symlinks, updates are live and reconcile is idempotent.
meta/develop: ADR aspiration without evidence
An ADR accepted from reasoning alone about an external system is an aspiration wearing a decision's clothes.
ADR is one stage, not the whole method
The loop is deliberately not ADR-driven development: prose claims such as ADRs, design notes, and specs must be held to evidence from the running system.
ADR-first
Front order used when the direction is the point: the shape is known and the decision must be on record before others build on it.
Choose front order by location of uncertainty
Rule that the front order is picked by where the uncertainty lives (artifacts, instructions, external world), with the stage answering the load-bearing question going first.
Delegation to stage skills
