Retrieved content and tool output are treated as data, and the tester is the first target of injection.
Unscoped test as data incident
Testing without a defined scope can expose real user data, constituting a data incident and potentially a crime.
Verified-good controls
A report section recording controls that held, distinguishing sound surfaces from untested ones.
softwaredev/code/security/secrets: Committed means compromised
A secret that reached version control is considered compromised immediately; removal from file or history is hygiene, not remedy.
Credential rotation
The remedy for a compromised secret, performed in descending blast-radius order (signing keys, datastore credentials, third-party tokens) under explicit confirmation.
Establish secret existence via metadata
Confirming a secret exists using metadata such as filename or scanner hit without opening it, to avoid placing live bytes in a transcript.
Extract hardcoded secret to environment variable
Remediation procedure for a hardcoded secret: move it to an environment variable, flag it, and check git history.
History rewrite is an owner decision
Rewriting git history to remove a secret is a decision belonging to the repository owner.
Never commit secret files
Rule prohibiting committing files with real secrets, API keys, tokens, passwords, private keys, and certificates to version control.
Password hashing
Passwords must be hashed using bcrypt or argon2 with an appropriate work factor, never stored in plain text, and never with self-rolled hashing.
Placeholder example config
Practice of creating a template file with placeholder values alongside a real secrets file, and ensuring the real file is gitignored.
Record credentials by key name and location only
Artifacts such as logs, tickets, and chat replies should reference credentials only by key name and location, never by value, even partially masked.
Secret scan as rotation exit gate
Re-running the secret scan after each rotation to verify completion.
softwaredev/code/supplychain: Assessment tiers
An ordered set of assessment levels from fast and cheap to slow and thorough: maturity, repo audit, source audit, dep scan, automation, history sever.
Automation (Tier 4)
Integrating scanning into CI or Makefile for established projects.
Check what a package is before safety
Principle that one should verify what a package actually is before whether it is safe, since a thin wrapper around a mature library is usually the wrong adoption even if safe.
Containers aren't a security boundary
Principle that running code in Docker does not protect against malicious code, e.g. a malicious setup.py still has network access.
Dependency scan (Tier 3)
Scanning dependencies for known vulnerabilities before installing them.
History sever (Tier 5)
Flattening or deleting tainted git history when the history itself is the threat.
Match the tool to the project
Principle to choose scanning tooling proportional to project scale: manual for hobby projects, GitHub Actions for team repos, without skipping levels or overbuilding.
Maturity check (Tier 0)
A quick check of whether a package is what it presents itself as, performed before adopting anything found via search.
Repo audit (Tier 1)
A seconds-long check of git history, size, and leaked secrets in any unfamiliar repository.
Responsible disclosure
Reporting leaked secrets found in someone else's repo privately with masked values and remediation hints rather than a public callout.
Scan before you run
Principle that dependencies or code from unfamiliar sources must be inspected before installing or executing, since installation and execution can run arbitrary code.
Source audit (Tier 2)
A review of source code for dangerous code patterns before running anything.
Supply chain trust assessment
A tiered process for evaluating whether unfamiliar code, repositories, and dependencies can be trusted before running or installing them.
softwaredev/code/supplychain/automation: GitHub's code scanning tool, suited for team or production-facing projects with CI for continuous monitoring.
A GitHub service configured by a file that opens pull requests for outdated or vulnerable dependencies.
Progression from manual scans to Makefile, to GitHub Action, to Dependabot/CodeQL, triggered by specific needs; levels should not be skipped.
A CI workflow using free, open source GitHub Actions to run scanners for projects that have CI or collaborators.
The simplest scanning automation: a Makefile target that wraps the appropriate scanner.
Running scanners manually when it matters, appropriate for solo or exploratory projects.
Match scanning approach to project maturity
Principle that the scanning automation proposed should fit the project's current state, e.g., not proposing CodeQL where there is no CI.
Review Dependabot PRs; no blind auto-merge
Dependabot pull requests should be reviewed rather than auto-merged blindly.
Adding software bill of materials generation to the release workflow when compliance or procurement requires it.
softwaredev/code/supplychain/depscan: Dev dependencies carry lower risk than runtime dependencies.
Package installation executes arbitrary code (e.g., install scripts), making it a security risk that motivates scanning beforehand.
Scanning a project's lockfiles for known vulnerable or malicious dependencies before installing them.
Checking whether a fixed version exists, and updating if so.
Choosing an appropriate scanner per ecosystem, preferring tools already available or trivial to install.
Assessing vulnerability findings by reachability, patch availability, dependency type, and severity rather than treating every CVE as a blocker.
Checking whether the project actually uses the vulnerable code in a dependency.
Rust vulnerability scanner using the RustSec advisory database.
Official Go team vulnerability scanning tool.
Built-in Node.js vulnerability audit command shipped with npm, requiring no extra install.
Google-backed multi-ecosystem vulnerability scanner that queries OSV.dev; recommended default.
Official PyPA vulnerability scanner for Python that uses the PyPI advisory database.
softwaredev/code/supplychain/depscan/go: Go's checksum database (sum.golang.org) provides transparency so that published modules cannot be silently altered after publication.
Replace directives in Go module files can redirect dependencies to arbitrary local paths or forks, potentially substituting unexpected code.
A set of supply chain risks and safeguards particular to the Go ecosystem, including module replacement, code generation and remote installs.
Install from URL downloads and compiles in one step
Installing a Go program directly from a URL downloads and compiles the source in a single step, so users should know the source.
The practice of inspecting source or directives before executing them to avoid running untrusted commands.
Generate comments in Go source files execute whatever command follows them, so they can run arbitrary code when invoked.
softwaredev/code/supplychain/depscan/nod: Ignore-scripts option
An installation option that skips running package scripts, reducing risk but potentially breaking legitimate packages that need them.
Lifecycle scripts run on install
npm packages can define scripts in package.json (e.g., postinstall) that run automatically during installation, executing arbitrary code.
Node-specific supply chain risks
Security risks specific to the Node/npm ecosystem, including install scripts, npx, transitive dependencies and typosquatting.
Run packages without installing (npx)
Running packages directly without a separate install step, which downloads and executes code in one step.
Transitive dependencies as attack surface
Indirect dependencies of a project vastly outnumber direct ones and constitute the main supply chain attack surface.
Typosquatting
Attack in which malicious packages are published with names similar to popular packages to trick users into installing them.
Verify package names and download counts
Mitigation practice of checking package name spelling and download counts on npmjs.com before installing.
Caret version ranges
Semver range specifiers that tell the package manager to resolve the latest compatible version, allowing new releases to be installed automatically.
Compromised patch release risk
The risk that a malicious or compromised patch version published briefly can silently land in a project via automatic resolution.
Delay adoption of brand-new package versions
Waiting (e.g., under 48 hours) before adopting newly published package versions so the community can vet them.
Exact version pinning in package.json
Specifying exact versions for direct dependencies rather than ranges when generating package.json.
Follow existing convention but flag trade-off
When a project already uses caret ranges, follow its convention while flagging the security trade-off.
Investigate new transitive dependencies
New transitive dependencies appearing in a lockfile update are a signal to investigate before committing.
Lockfile as defense
Lockfiles record exactly what dependencies resolved so new versions only arrive upon deliberate update.
Lockfile hygiene
The practice of pinning dependencies via lockfiles to trusted versions and knowing what was pinned so issues can be traced.
Review lockfile diff
Inspecting the lockfile diff after installing or updating dependencies to spot packages not requested.
Use lockfile-respecting install in CI
Using npm ci-style installs that respect the lockfile exactly rather than resolving new versions in CI and reproducible builds.
softwaredev/code/supplychain/depscan/pyt: Even safer declarative packaging formats can specify build backends that execute code during installation.
Package names in copied requirements files should be checked carefully to avoid typosquatted dependencies.
Python pickle files can execute arbitrary Python code when loaded, so unpickling untrusted data is unsafe.
Supply chain security risks particular to the Python ecosystem, including install-time code execution, pickle deserialization, and PyPI typosquatting.
Attack in which malicious packages are published with names similar to popular packages to trick users into installing them.
softwaredev/code/supplychain/depscan/rus: Build script runs at compile time
A Rust build script (build.rs) executes at compile time with full system access, so it can run arbitrary code on the build machine.
Proc macros are compile-time code execution
Procedural macro crates run arbitrary code during compilation.
Rust supply chain healthier but not immune
Rust's ecosystem is smaller with stronger safety norms than npm/PyPI, but typosquatting and maintainer compromise still occur.
Supply chain security risks particular to the Rust ecosystem, including build scripts, unsafe code, and proc macros.
Unsafe blocks bypass the borrow checker
Unsafe blocks in Rust bypass the borrow checker; not inherently malicious but worth reviewing in unfamiliar code.
softwaredev/code/supplychain/historyseve: Using BFG Repo-Cleaner to retain history while removing specific secrets or large files; much faster than git filter-branch.
A .git directory bloated with unneeded artifacts, a reason to sever history.
GitHub forks share git objects with upstream through the fork network, creating a trust chain to the original author's objects.
Breaking a GitHub fork's relationship with upstream by cloning locally, deleting the fork, creating a new standalone repo, and pushing the clone.
A history-severing technique that keeps only the current tree state in a new orphan branch and discards all prior commit history.
A clean break of provenance from an untrusted source repository, achieved by severing history or the fork relationship.
Malicious payloads or suspicious content in an upstream repository's commit history, a reason to sever.
Secrets in git history that cannot be rotated, such as revoked keys still in git objects, which motivate severing history.
softwaredev/code/supplychain/maturity: Agent-generated packages weaken search rank signal
Coding agents make competent, documented, new, barely used packages cheap, weakening the correlation of polish with adoption and maturity.
Hand-rolling as supply-chain choice

Building something yourself shifts maintenance and defect surface onto you; a maintained library is warranted for specification-heavy problems such as parsing formats, dates/time zones, encodings, cryptography, and protocols.
High adoption carries its own risk
Widely used packages attract more attacker attention, so the other supply-chain tiers remain necessary.
Low adoption asks a question
Low download counts cannot distinguish new, narrow, and excellent packages, so one must inspect what is underneath.
Order-of-magnitude adoption gap
A large difference in adoption between a wrapper and its dependency, which shifts the burden onto the wrapper to justify itself.
Prefer the layer doing the work
When a wrapper and its dependency both solve the problem, the dependency is usually smaller, better-tested, and longer-lived.
Presentation outruns adoption
A failure mode where polished READMEs, benchmarks, and feature lists are cheap to produce and no longer signal real-world usage or exposure to real inputs.
Read the manifest for wrapper tell
Inspecting a package's manifest; a short dependency list with one substantial entry indicates a wrapper.
Registry adoption metrics over stars
Using registry API data (total downloads, recent downloads, first-published date) to gauge adoption, since stars reflect attention rather than reliance.
Skepticism toward your own output
Applying the same scrutiny to code you wrote recently, since a new library and a battle-tested one look alike in a README but carry different risk.
Thin wrapper positioned as first-order tool
A package whose substantive work happens in a dependency, yet is presented as a primary tool; the dependency can often be used directly with more adoption and a smaller surface.
Three-question appropriateness check
A minute-long pre-adoption check: how many people use the package, what is underneath it, and how the wrapped dependency's adoption compares.
Unknown specification defects surface slowly
In specification-bound problems, defects lie in parts of the spec the author did not know to handle and surface one at a time in review long after the work seems finished.
softwaredev/code/supplychain/repoaudit: The common secret leak pattern where a developer commits a file, then adds it to .gitignore, leaving it in git history.
A quick check comparing the size of the .git directory to the working tree to detect hidden large content in history.
Binary blobs, database dumps, or zip archives stored in git history that inflate the repository.
A seconds-long check of git history, size, and leaked secrets in any unfamiliar repository.
Reporting leaked secrets found in someone else's repo privately with masked values and remediation hints rather than a public callout.
Searching git history diffs for common credential patterns to find leaked credentials.
softwaredev/code/supplychain/sourceaudit: Eval/exec usage is not inherently malicious (template engines, REPLs) and is suspicious only in specific contexts such as install-time scripts, decode-then-execute code, or files unrelated to the project's purpose.
A list of code patterns paired with their associated risks, such as arbitrary execution, obfuscated payloads, deserialization RCE, shell injection, and data exfiltration.
Remote code execution risk arising from deserializing untrusted data.
Use of decode operations to conceal and later reveal malicious payloads.
Outbound HTTP in setup as exfiltration risk
Network calls made during setup or install code indicate a potential data exfiltration risk.
Risk of attacker-controlled input being executed by a shell.
Clusters of single-character variable names with hex or encoded strings indicate intentional obfuscation.
Scanning unfamiliar source code for dangerous patterns before running it, in a language-agnostic way.
softwaredev/code/testing: Arrange-Act-Assert
A test structure consisting of setup, call, and verification steps.
Assert only observable behavior
Assertions should target observable outputs and side effects, not method call counts or internal/private state.
Boundary value testing
Testing min, max, off-by-one, and empty collection values for a function.
Contract test
Test level proving an endpoint, message, or structured output matches its published schema.
End-to-end test
Test level proving a critical user flow works through the whole stack; one or two per flow.
Evaluation test
Test showing model behavior meets a rubric at a stated pass threshold.
Golden test
Test proving a deterministic transform, prompt, or renderer still produces the reviewed baseline.
Ground truth golden-master baseline
Golden-master baseline captured before a refactor or migration.
Integration test
Test level proving code crosses a real adapter (database, file, network, SDK, model) correctly.
Lowest test level that proves the contract
Choose the lowest test level that proves the contract; mismatched levels (mock-heavy unit tests, e2e for pure functions) are misplaced.
Mocking
Related way covering when and how to mock dependencies.
One logical assertion per test
Each test verifies one behavior rather than one line.
Property test
Test proving an algorithm holds an invariant across generated inputs.
Synthetic test data
Fixtures, seed data, demo environments and prompt examples are generated to match real shape and constraints without being real records; masking is not anonymization.
Test coverage categories per function
For each function under test, cover happy path, empty/null input, boundary values, and error conditions.
Test framework detection
Detect the test framework from project files and follow its conventions for file placement and naming.
Test independence
Tests must not share mutable state with one another.
Test-driven development
Related way covering the TDD cycle.
Testing evaluation way
Reproduce as reported, drive the real path, re-review fixes, count what ran.
Testing gates
Every gate reports executed, discovered, or absent; a zero needs a positive control.
Unit test
Test level proving pure logic such as a transformation, parser, or validator gives the right output.
softwaredev/code/testing/evaluation: Common rationalizations
Table of excuses for skipping injection protection paired with counters.
Count what ran
A pass count must carry its denominator; reports state the command, number of runs, and whether the failure reproduced before the fix.
Drive the path users take
A test reaches its state the way the real program does, letting the real loop make calls rather than invoking internals by hand.
Evaluation loop
A run that decides whether a fix or a test is done, consisting of reproducing the failure, driving the real path, re-reviewing each fix, and counting what ran.
Fix every finding, then re-review
Remediate each finding, then review again by replaying each finding's original scenario against the fixed code, continuing while rounds still find defects.
Flaky failure run-count statistics
A flake failing 2 in 300 runs passes 20 consecutive runs about seven times in eight, so 20/20 usually misses it; loop until failure and run a multiple of that count after the fix.
Headless driver keeps real cadence
A headless test driver fires draws, timers, ticks and redraws in the same order and under the same conditions as the interactive run.
Plant the defect to prove the test can see it
A fifth move, in the gates way, where a defect is planted so that a test is seen failing.
Reproduce the failure as reported
Checking a fix against the failure the reporter saw, using the reporter's inputs, paths, sizes, versions, configuration and environment.
Test-only entry point is part of the subject
A test-only entry point or flag must run the same code as the user's path, or else the user's path should be driven instead.
Unreproduced means unverified
If a failure could not be reproduced, record it as unreproduced and unverified rather than trusting that the fix looks right.
softwaredev/code/testing/evaluation/scre: Assertions way
Way covering golden baselines, masked volatile leaves, and the enumerated-delta rule, deciding whether each change is accepted.
Capture at user terminal sizes
Capturing each screen at a small and a common terminal size (e.g., 80x25 and 100x30), adding sizes named in reports, to reveal layout defects at the edges.
Layout defects at the edges
Defects such as wrapped lines, footers pushed off the bottom, truncated columns, and modals wider than the terminal.
Mocking way
Way covering test doubles for the commands a stand-in runner replaces.
Row-by-row golden diff review
Reading each changed golden image or text capture row by row, naming what moved in each changed row and confirming the capture shows the state its name claims.
Screen evaluation
Evaluating a terminal screen by viewing it in the states and at the sizes users actually reach, using a multiplexer or pseudo-terminal harness.
Scripted keys to reach states
Scripting the key sequence that reaches each state under test and storing it beside the golden image, driving the real input loop.
Stand-in runner for external commands
A fixture-held substitute for an external command that deliberately produces edge cases, e.g., 25 long lines and exit status 3, to exercise wrapping, scrolling, overflow, and error paths.
Terminal multiplexer or pty harness capture
Running the program in a private session under a terminal multiplexer or pseudo-terminal harness, sending keys, and capturing the pane as text or image.
Testing evaluation way
Reproduce as reported, drive the real path, re-review fixes, count what ran.
softwaredev/code/testing/gates: Absent state
A gate state meaning no such gate exists, recorded with a date and a reason.
Assertions way
Way covering golden baselines, masked volatile leaves, and the enumerated-delta rule, deciding whether each change is accepted.
Cheap gates first
Run cheap syntactic gates first and proceed to slower ones only when they pass; avoid broad batteries on provably local changes.
Code testing way
Way covering testing, coverage, fixtures, test structure and coverage.
Discovered state
A gate known to exist but deliberately left unrun, reported with the reason it was skipped. Includes zero-exit runs that did no work.
Executed state
A gate run on this change with prerequisites held and assertions executed; reported with the command and result.
Gate depth follows change class
The minimum depth of gates run scales with the class of change, from a single focused check for trivial edits to broad system gates for auth, security, migration, or concurrency changes.
Inherited codebase full absent report
A codebase without test infrastructure still gets a full report with each standard gate listed as absent with a date.
Instrument is the first suspect
When a check and its subject disagree, read the raw source before recording a finding, since the measuring method may be at fault.
Measure effective state through real client path
A gate should measure effective state read back through the path a real client takes, since shortcuts miss faults in skipped paths and a control's presence in code does not prove wiring.
Never satisfy a check by changing what it measures
Do not remove the observed value, edit the declaration it reads, or revert the tripping change; update the assertion if the product deliberately changed, or fix the defect.
Planted violation earns trust for a new gate
A new gate earns trust once a planted violation has turned it red and the plant's removal has turned it green.
Positive control for zero results
A zero result (no findings, no hits, nothing collected) is reported only alongside a positive control that the same run detected, establishing the coverage.
Recovery way
An environment guidance area covering recovery from failures in software development, including handling repeated gate failures.
Report format and unverified closing
The report lists one line per gate with state first and closes with what was deliberately left unverified, distinguishing blocked from skipped, so a partial pass never reads as completion.
Silent disabling is a hidden absent
Disabling a flaky gate without recording it conceals a missing gate; fix the flake or record the gate as discovered with the reason.
Silent verification failure
The quiet failure where a suite was never invoked, a step skipped itself, or a scanner hit the wrong path and the report omits it, so the reader takes silence for a pass.
Three-state gate reporting
Every considered gate is reported in exactly one of three states: executed, discovered, or absent, each with required supporting information.
Wrongly sized increment
A development increment that is too large or otherwise mis-sized, indicated when a gate fails red twice.
Zero exit code is not proof of execution
An exit code of zero counts as executed only when the check did its work; self-skipped steps, zero-test collections, inert tools, or short test counts are recorded as discovered.
Zero-count failure in authored checks
A check you author counts what it examined and fails when that count is zero inside its own perimeter, treating an empty glob as an environment fault.
softwaredev/code/testing/gates/assertion: Assert composition, not only a count
Assertions should check what a result is made of (names, keys, ordered members, full set difference) rather than only its count, since offsetting errors preserve counts.
Assert destination, content, or argument
Instead of call counts, assert on the destination, content, or argument passed to the collaborator; counts are valid only when the count is the promised behavior.
Assertion shape
The structure of a test assertion that determines whether it can actually detect the defect it was written to catch.
Echo vs witness
A duplicate that could be changed by one coordinated edit with nothing failing is an echo; a copy that would fail on change is a witness kept on purpose.
Failure identifies what drifted
Assert each dimension under its own name so a failure identifies the property that moved, rather than one assertion over a serialized blob.
Golden and snapshot assertions

Snapshots are assertions whose expected side was captured from the subject; they are witnesses only after reviewed baselines, captured pre-change with volatile leaves masked and only enumerated intended deltas allowed.
Independent expected value
Expected values must be independent of the subject under test, written as literals or verified by joins across independently maintained sources, to avoid echoes.
Mock invocation count assertion
Asserting only how many times a mock was called is a canonical vacuous assertion, passing even when the collaborator is called for a wrong reason.
No regression on red baseline by failing-test names
Establish no regression on a red baseline by comparing names of failing tests before and after, and report new coverage as a delta.
Passing gate can prove nothing
A gate that executes and asserts can still stay green through the bug it was meant to catch.
Re-recording snapshot
Re-recording a snapshot to make it pass turns the baseline back into an echo.
Self-expiring known-bug marker
A named assertion of today's broken behavior that passes while the bug lives and fails when the bug is fixed, forcing the assertion to be tightened and retiring the debt.
Skipped or relaxed tests hide bugs
Skipping or weakening a test, especially a skip without reason and ticket, hides a known hole in coverage.
softwaredev/code/testing/mocking: Do not mock code under test or internal helpers
Guideline that the code being tested and its internal helpers should not be mocked.
Do not mock things you control
Guideline to avoid mocking anything you control and can test directly.
Do not mock value objects or simple data structures
Guideline against mocking value objects and simple data structures, which can be used directly.
Fakes are robust to implementation changes
Fakes don't break when implementation details change, unlike mocks.
Fakes exercise real behavior
Fakes run real behavior, whereas mocks only verify method calls.
Flaky tests
Tests that pass or fail inconsistently, here caused by shared mock state.
Mock external dependencies
Practice of mocking things outside the code's control such as network, filesystem, databases, and third-party APIs.
Mock invocation count assertion
Asserting only how many times a mock was called is a canonical vacuous assertion, passing even when the collaborator is called for a wrong reason.
Mock slow or non-deterministic operations
Practice of mocking operations like time, randomness, and system calls that are slow or yield non-repeatable results.
Prefer fakes over mocks
Guideline favoring in-memory fake implementations over mock libraries because they are more reliable.
Reset mocks between tests
Practice of resetting mock state between tests because shared mock state causes flaky tests.
Too many mocks signals too many dependencies
Needing more than 3 mocks in a test indicates the code has too many dependencies and should be refactored first.
Use mock libraries only when fakes too complex
Mock libraries are reserved for cases where writing a fake would be too complex.
softwaredev/code/testing/tdd: Bug fix via test that would have caught it
Writing a test that would have caught a bug before fixing it.
Characterization test
A test written on untested inherited code that asserts current behavior, defects included, rather than a guessed correct answer.
Common TDD rationalizations
A table of excuses for skipping tests paired with counters.
Green phase
Writing the minimum code necessary to make the failing test pass.
Proving an inherited green suite by reintroducing defects
Verifying an inherited passing suite by reintroducing a past defect in production code, confirming the suite fails for that reason, then reverting.
Red phase
Writing a failing test that describes the desired behavior.
Red-Green-Refactor cycle
The three-step TDD cycle: write a failing test, write minimal code to pass it, then refactor while tests still pass.
Refactor phase
Cleaning up code without changing behavior, with tests still passing.
Untested code first workflow
Procedure for inherited code lacking tests or spec: write a characterization test, run it to pass, make the change so it fails as the intended RED, then resume the cycle.
When TDD applies
Situations suited to TDD: new functions with clear contracts, bug fixes, and refactors needing behavior-preservation confidence.
When TDD doesn't apply
Situations where TDD is not suited: exploratory prototyping, pure UI layout, and glue code.
softwaredev/delivery: Check Makefile targets before ad-hoc commands
Guidance to inspect a project's Makefile for targets that encode the actual publishing workflow before running ad-hoc commands.
Child way covering commit structure and commit messages (delivery/commits).
A parent way covering the journey from local changes to production, including commits, PRs, releases, patches, and planning.
Child way covering PRs, issues, review, and merge strategy (delivery/github).
Child way covering readiness of an area (build, verify, deliver, recover) before adding primitives or changing it.
Child way covering planning of implementation (delivery/implement).
Child way covering patch creation as a delivery stage.
Child way covering releases, tagging, and publishing.
The design, numbering, idempotency, and consolidation practices for schema migrations, now housed in the data domain rather than delivery.
softwaredev/delivery/branching: A branch can be pushed and left, serving as a draft of a pull request and enabling clean context switching between tasks.
Branches make work reversible without history-rewriting gymnastics, whereas committing to main on public repos leaves force-push as the only undo.
Guidance (not a gate) to create a branch when making substantial changes rather than working directly on main.
Branch names use prefixes matching conventional commit types, and are short, lowercase, and hyphen-separated; the name often becomes the PR title.
Practice of glancing at the displayed git branch and state before making edits, to know where work is landing.
Main is fine for lightweight edits
Exploration, temporary edits, and quick config tweaks can be done on main without branching.
softwaredev/delivery/commits: The practice of making each commit contain exactly one logical change.
Branch names use prefixes matching conventional commit types, and are short, lowercase, and hyphen-separated; the name often becomes the PR title.
A commit message convention using typed prefixes (feature, fix, docs, refactor, test, chore) and scopes matching the area of change.
Child way covering PRs, issues, review, and merge strategy (delivery/github).
Guidance to document the reasoning behind decisions rather than code changes, since git records the code changes.
The delivery/release way, in which commit types drive version bumps.
A rule to omit Co-Authored-By lines and emoji trailers from commit messages.
softwaredev/delivery/github: When the user says 'merge it' without a strategy, ask whether to regular merge or squash.
Every change lands through a PR
Policy that all changes, including solo projects, are merged via pull requests, which serve as a decision record and CI gate.
Use issues for requirements and bugs with a basic label set, avoiding project boards and milestone hierarchies; clarify ambiguous 'issue'.
Rebase-merge is avoided because it rewrites authorship and timestamps.
PR description scaled to team size
PR detail scales with contributors: title and bullets for solo/pair, context/reviewers/issues for teams, automated review for three or more.
Steps performed after every merge to tidy up the repository state.
Default merge strategy that preserves the branch's narrative commit history on main; squash only for single-purpose branches with commit noise.
A macro that checks repository configuration (README, license, templates, branch protection, badges) and reports gaps, with fixes offered within user rights.
Practice of reviewing after opening the PR without waiting to be asked, with depth scaled to blast radius and operator approval gating direction-setting work.
softwaredev/delivery/groundwork: Build condition
One command produces the artifact from a clean checkout.
Capture working process in project instructions
Once an area meets the four conditions, the working commands, gates, and deploy path are recorded in the project instructions.
Deliver condition
One repeatable path moves the artifact to a test environment and to production.
Deliverable-first ordering
The order of work: make the area deliverable, then change it, then write instructions describing what now works.
Delivery implement way
Related way on the failing test and rollback path each task carries.
Environment recovery way
Related way on right-sizing an increment when gates go red.
Four conditions (Build, Verify, Deliver, Recover)
A table of conditions an area must satisfy before behaviour or contract changes: one-command build, automated CI-run verification, repeatable delivery path, and rehearsed rollback.
Ground truth baseline way
Related way for capturing the baseline before a refactor.
Groundwork child ways
Child ways covering contribution self-account versus demonstration, ordering open changes by readiness, work clustering on edit permissions, and tracing where a change waits.
Host parity way
Related way noting that a green result on the authoring host is evidence only about that host.
Host-dependent row is missing
A condition that depends on a person's memory or holds only on the authoring host counts as missing.
Knowledge authoring way
Meta way for writing instructions once the process exists.
Missing row as finding
When a condition row is missing, filling it is the first piece of work and it is reported as a finding rather than hidden by more agents or longer prompts.
Premature primitive

A skill, agent definition, prompt, or abstraction that describes a process that cannot yet run: no proving command, no repeatable deploy, no way back. It looks like progress while nothing customer-facing changes.
Recover condition
Rollback has run at least once, on purpose.
Testing gates
Every gate reports executed, discovered, or absent; a zero needs a positive control.
Trivial edit exemption
A trivial edit with no behaviour surface needs only one focused check and skips the four-conditions table.
Verify condition
Automated checks exercise the existing behaviour about to be touched, and they run in CI.
Writing the change is the short part
Writing the change is a small portion of getting it to a customer; the wait lies in review, environment request, approval and release window, which new primitives do not address.
softwaredev/delivery/groundwork/claims: Adversarial refutation pass on finished deliverable
A pass run by a separate agent on a finished deliverable, working from primary sources and stopping at could-not-refute; this way applies the same posture during ongoing work.
Common rationalizations for trusting claims
A table of excuses for accepting claims without evidence (thorough description, experienced author, green CI, issue not code, agent said tests are good) with counters.
Contributions as claims
The principle that every contribution (PR description, issue, agent report) is a claim about its own value, and the artifact is not evidence for the claim merely by being well written.
Grade the evidence, not the polish
Evaluation stance that polished writeups only indicate author care and say nothing about whether the change works.
Green CI does not establish truth
Passing CI shows the intended path ran, not that the claim is true.
Issues are checkable claims
An issue asserts that a defect exists and matters, and both assertions are checkable.
Our own reports are claims too
Agent and internal reports, such as claims of comprehensive tests, are the same class of statement as contributor claims and must report what ran and what it would have caught.
Snapshot test encodes current behavior
A test written by copying the current output proves the code does what it does and can preserve a bug when requirement and implementation disagree.
What does this claim?
First review question: state the contribution's claim in one sentence in the reviewer's own words.
What would show the claim wrong?

Second review question: identify what would falsify the claim and whether the contribution includes it, e.g. a test failing on revert, a reproduction going green, or a measured number with its command.
Who other than the author has run it?
Third review question: whether anyone besides the author has tried to break the claim; a claim nobody has tried to break has been read, not reviewed.
softwaredev/delivery/groundwork/permissi: Excuses such as 'it's the platform team's backlog' or 'a wrapper gets us past it' that justify not reporting the boundary.
Do not compensate with a primitive
Avoid adding another agent, longer prompt, or wrapper around a broken step, since it hides the boundary and adds maintenance burden.
Hand the decision to a person
Surface the boundary to a human as a choice: who must approve, what commitment moves, and how soon return is wanted.
Improving the periphery while the core is untestable
Improving reachable peripheral artifacts while the core remains untestable is the pattern the approach aims to stop.
Name the boundary as a finding
When hitting a boundary, record which condition is missing, who owns the fix, and what decision or access is needed.
People tend to work on what they have permission to change, so improvement concentrates where access is easy rather than where it is needed.
A pattern where the work queue is heavy with peripheral items (docs, config, adapters, prompts, abstractions) while the underlying layer goes untouched.
If a leader must step in each time to get a change deployed, that dependency is itself a missing condition to be reported.
softwaredev/delivery/groundwork/sequence: Anti-pattern: ranking by argument quality
Ranking items by how well they are argued rather than by what they make possible.
Anti-pattern: stacking behaviour changes into unverifiable area
Merging a stack of small behaviour changes into an area that cannot be verified, justified because each is small.
Anti-pattern: tests after the queue clears
Deferring writing tests until after queued changes land, which makes it hard to tell which change broke things.
Common rationalizations for skipping holds
Typical justifications for merging into unready areas, each paired with a counter.
Establishing items jump the queue
Items that establish a missing condition (test command, CI, repeatable deploy, rollback) are prioritized ahead of others.
Hold with prerequisite
Items that assume an unmet condition are held with the prerequisite named, as a state with an owner and exit condition.
Normal review depth
Items touching an area meeting all four conditions receive normal review depth chosen by the merge coverage axis.
Order in the Queue
A way governing the sequencing of open items, holding changes that assume unmet conditions and prioritizing those that establish them.
Premature
A change that is individually good but wrong to accept now because of ordering relative to missing conditions.
Quiet drop
A hold without an exit condition, which effectively drops the item silently.
Triage by readiness
Practice of naming the area each open item touches, checking it against the four conditions, and placing the item accordingly.
Verify condition
One of the four conditions: the ability to verify behaviour in an area, e.g., via a test command.
softwaredev/delivery/groundwork/stall: Aim at the longest wait
Directing improvement effort at the longest waiting period in the delivery of a change rather than at the working time of writing it.
Automating the fast part
Adding automation to the already fast coding step, which makes coding faster without making delivery faster.
Decision waits belong to a person
If the longest wait is a decision, the finding is a decision owned by a person; more tests or agents cannot resolve it.
Follow One Change
A diagnostic practice of picking a single change and walking it from a clean checkout into production with the people who did it, recording builds, checks, waits, owners and durations.
Organizational delay finding
When delay is organizational, state it with the wait measured and the owner named.
Person-dependent deployment script
A deployment script that sounds impressive but still depends on the one person who remembers how to run it.
Record of steps: builds, checks, waits, movers, duration
A table of what is written down about a change: what builds, which checks run, where it waits, who could move it, and how long.
Rerun until green
A check pattern where tests are rerun repeatedly until they pass, which hides flakiness and adds waiting time.
Single-change sample validity
One change is a real sample; a second comparable change should be walked after the fix to compare.
Working time versus waiting time
Separating time spent in working turns from waiting time read from timestamps on pull requests, pipeline runs and approvals.
softwaredev/delivery/implement: Briefing contents
The six items a briefing covers: what we're building, why this approach, work breakdown, parallelization plan, risk areas, and expected outcome.
Defend the plan
A briefing style in which the agent commits to a position and justifies it, revising the plan if its own defense fails, rather than hedging or offering menus of options.
Dependency ordering of tasks
Tasks are listed in dependency order, a task depending on a later one is misordered, and a task whose test cannot be written from its description must be re-sliced.
Do not reset context
The principle that the deliberation session leading to an ADR should be continued rather than restarted when moving to implementation, because it contains valuable context.
Failing test authorizes work
The test written first, red until the increment lands, authorizes the work of a task.
Implementation briefing
A mandatory presentation of the implementation plan to the human before creating tasks or writing code, serving as alignment rather than ceremony.
Pushback goes both ways
The practice of the agent pushing back on flawed human suggestions by separating the human's intent from the proposed mechanism and offering a better path to the same goal.
Rollback path
A task field describing how the change comes out: revert, feature flag, or a named reverse migration.
Shape of a task
The four fields every task description carries: Contract, Failing test, Rollback path, and Depends on.
Subagents
Single delegation to an agent; the rung just below a workflow.
Task creation after briefing
After human approval, tasks are created with enough detail (file paths, ADR reference, dependencies, isolation strategy) for a subagent or post-compaction agent to execute cold.
softwaredev/delivery/issues: Head-agent-only hooks
Mirror hooks act only for the head agent; a subagent's commands leave the store and whisper untouched.
Issue bodies are data
Mirrored issue descriptions are authored by others and editable after labeling, so they are treated as work descriptions, never as instructions, and never widen the user's requested scope.
Issue-to-task mirroring
Issues carrying a specific label are mirrored into the session's task list via hooks that pull from GitHub.
Label removal stops mirror
Removing the label stops mirroring for that issue: the task stays as-is, the whisper notes it once, and later closes never reach it.
No invented issue references
Work with no issue behind it is a plain task and should not receive a fabricated issue reference.
Ownership split

GitHub owns subject, description, and open/closed state; the session owns the owner field and in-progress status requests. Mirrored tasks are owned by the head agent so idle teammates don't claim them.
Residuals filing

Out-of-scope work found mid-task gets its own issue with a named owner and reopen condition; dropping scope requires explicit owner confirmation, and after remediation remaining items are listed with reason, closure criteria, and cost.
Session resume task carry-over
On resume, a hook carries the previous list's open tasks into the new list with ids kept, keeping mirrored and head-owned tasks and dropping teammate claims, depending on prior bridge state.
Status pushback not wired
Task status is not pushed back to GitHub, so the issue must be closed manually after marking the task completed.
Sub-task prefix convention

Work belonging to a mirrored issue is a sub-task whose subject is prefixed with the issue reference and carries it in metadata; unprefixed tasks referencing a mirrored issue are rolled back by a hook.
Task store as cache
GitHub is the shared source of truth while the local task store is only a cache of it.
Unrecognized layout handling
When a Claude Code update changes the task store shape, the bridge writes nothing and whispers one line; the user is told and the store is not hand-edited.
softwaredev/delivery/merge: Code-reviewer subagent
The subagent spawned at the merge gate to perform review; the operator has a built-in manual equivalent.
Dispatch reviewer rather than re-request permission
Asking to merge is asking for the review the gate specifies; dispatch the reviewer instead of re-requesting permission, naming the payoff. The ambiguity is which corner, never whether to review.
Four-square review classification
A classification of increments on two axes (machine review depth and human gate) yielding four paths: run it, swarm-gate, review + offer, full gate.
Human gate axis (direction-setting / unread)
The Y axis, driven by whether the work sets direction and whether the operator has already read it, determining whether human approval is needed.
Ledger drift audit example
An August 2026 audit found seventeen ADRs still Proposed or similar with implementation shipped, and four abandoned or solved documents, because the archive command was never run.
Machine review axis (complexity and blast-radius)
The X axis, driven by diff size, number of files, core-vs-leaf, test coverage and reversibility, determining light versus deep/swarm review.
Merging as stable tail of develop loop
Landing an increment is the stable tail of the develop loop: review, fix, merge, clean up.
Reconcile the decision ledger
At merge, flip the authorizing ADR's status to its shipped state and archive superseded or unnecessary ADRs in the same pass as cleanup.
Remediate before you merge
Findings from review must be fixed or declined with a recorded reason per finding before the merge gate; known findings are not carried past it.
Repository enforcement decides first

The repository's mechanical review policy (rulesets, protected branches, CODEOWNERS, status checks, hooks) takes precedence; judgement can add review but never subtract. If unreadable, review is required.
Surface ambiguous classification
When classification is ambiguous, surface the call rather than silently picking a corner; bias autonomous inside a loop, ask outside.
Version bumps merge on green CI
A release bump PR whose diff is only the version line and lockfile entry merges once CI passes without review; bumps with anything else take the normal gate.
softwaredev/delivery/patches: Patches in a series are cumulative, with each patch assuming that all prior patches have been applied.
When changing an earlier patch alters context that later patches depend on, downstream patches fail to apply.
A golden rule stating that patches must be generated from real file changes using tooling rather than written manually.
A set of commands for tasks such as generating, applying, checking, reverting patches and comparing files.
The remedy for downstream failures: apply each patch in turn, capture it, and repeat to regenerate the series.
softwaredev/delivery/release: Check Makefile targets before ad-hoc commands
Guidance to inspect a project's Makefile for targets that encode the actual publishing workflow before running ad-hoc commands.
Four conditions (Build, Verify, Deliver, Recover)
A table of conditions an area must satisfy before behaviour or contract changes: one-command build, automated CI-run verification, repeatable delivery path, and rehearsed rollback.
Infer version bump from commits
Determine the semantic version bump (major/minor/patch) from commit messages since the last tag.
Irreversible step last
The irreversible release step (destructive migration, key rotation, column drop) is named as such and performed last after reversible steps are green.
Keep a Changelog format
Changelog format used for release notes generated from commits since the last tag.
Migration reverse path
Auto-applied migrations remain in place when the artifact is reverted, so whether a migration has a reverse path must be recorded in the runbook.
Promote what passed
The released artifact must be the byte-identical one that passed gates, identified by digest, not rebuilt at release time.
Publishing artifacts
Release artifacts are published to destinations such as GitHub Releases, npm, PyPI, Cargo, AUR, and container registries, with multi-platform binaries attached to one GitHub Release.
Reconcile issue tracker before tagging
Before tagging a release, the issue tracker is reconciled with what the release claims, since 'fixed in X' becomes a public claim at release time.
Rollback must be exercised
A rollback only exists once it has been run; backups and procedures are unverified until restored or executed, and absence is recorded explicitly.
Signed tags require operator handoff
When a project signs tags, the agent cannot supply the passphrase, so it should hand the exact tag command to the operator instead of retrying.
Tag-triggered CI release workflow
A CI workflow triggered by a tag builds each platform and creates the release; it should be checked before hand-building artifacts.
Two-step release under branch protection
With a protected main branch, the version bump goes through a PR and the tag is applied only after it merges; tagging is the single outward step.
Update version file
Detect the project's version file (package.json, Cargo.toml, pyproject.toml, version.txt) and update it.
Version bumps merge on green CI
A release bump PR whose diff is only the version line and lockfile entry merges once CI passes without review; bumps with anything else take the normal gate.
