softwaredev/environment/attend: Attend monitor process
Attend is the active awareness module for Claude Code sessions, running as a persistent background process via Monitor and surfacing environmental changes as notifications.
Attend sensors
The set of sensors attend polls on adaptive schedules: git, peers, processes, and keepwarm.
Autonomy to reply
Agents may reply to peers directly without asking operator permission, since the operator participates by running attend and can intervene via chat.
CLI is the contract
Attend owns its internal state; agents must use CLI commands rather than reaching into attend-owned paths, and should raise broken commands with the user.
Channels
An escape hatch for private channels in long-running coordinated work (ADR-173), rarely needed since default broadcast plus filtering suffices; messages are bound to project liveness (ADR-136).
Emission filter
Attend's filter that demotes low-magnitude chatter to stderr so Monitor only wakes sessions with actionable content.
Keepwarm notification handling
A keepwarm notification asks for a one-word reply with no tools and no investigation; arming is the operator's call, with auto-arming three hours after a paid cold write.
Keepwarm sensor
A sensor that issues one wake at 50 idle minutes while armed so the prompt cache is read before its hour lapses (ADR-182).
New topic / broadcast message command
Command used to start a new topic or broadcast unsolicited information when no peer message is in the inbox; defaults to broadcast to all peers.
Reply to peer command
Command used when a peer-message notification just arrived; it auto-threads to that peer's message without id or lookup.
Silence is a valid reply
Not every peer message requires a response; attend never escalates a message the agent chose to ignore.
Synchronized messaging guidance sources
Messaging guidance is kept in three synchronized files (SKILL.md primer, messaging.md runtime reheat, and attend.md just-in-time way) which must be updated together.
Two delivery conduits, one contract
Peer messages are delivered either by a Stop hook drain at turn end (ADR-172) or by the Monitor-hosted poller while idle, both sharing one seen-set so messages arrive once.
softwaredev/environment/bounded-executio: Absence of output is not completion
No output or a timeout does not indicate a job finished; stalled jobs print nothing.
Background run with output file or Monitor tool
Commands that follow logs or serve ports are run in the background on the Bash tool with output read from a file, or watched via the Monitor tool or bounded poll.
Claim running only on a liveness signal
Before reporting a server, watcher, or job as up or done, observe a liveness signal or completion marker such as a port answering, log line, persistent pid, artifact, or exit status.
Guard hook for bounded execution
A hook that refuses prompt, non-returning, and wrong-kill commands, shipped deactivated and enabled via one project settings line (ADR-181).
Kill matching the wrong process
Killing by name or pattern can match the current shell, a subagent, or an operator's process rather than the intended one.
Launch returned without work done
A launch that returned only proves the launch occurred, not that the work was completed or is running.
Never-returning command
A command that follows a log or serves a port and never exits on its own.
Non-interactive flag
Running commands that ask for input with flags that suppress prompts; if it fails, the credential or config is the problem.
Prompt-blocked command
A command that sits waiting on an interactive prompt for input, burning the tool timeout.
Raise timeout instead of backgrounding builds
For a known long build, raise the timeout parameter and run in foreground rather than backgrounding it, since backgrounded builds fail silently.
Stop a process by its pid
Find the pid first, confirm it is yours, then kill that pid, using a pid recorded by the harness or in a pidfile.
Tool timeout firing
The harness killed a foreground command at its bound, possibly leaving a build or install half applied.
softwaredev/environment/config: Files that store environment variable configuration locally, accompanied by an example file with placeholders and verified to be gitignored.
Files holding configuration values, with priority below environment variables and above defaults.
A priority ordering of configuration sources: environment variables override config files, which override default values.
Fallback configuration values with the lowest priority, provided where safe such as timeouts, ports, and log levels.
Runtime-supplied key-value settings that hold the highest priority among configuration sources.
Fail fast on missing required config
A required config value that is missing or malformed fails at startup with a non-zero exit naming every offender.
Practice of creating a template file with placeholder values alongside a real secrets file, and ensuring the real file is gitignored.
Secrets belong in config, not code
Principle that secrets should be stored in configuration rather than hardcoded in source code.
A guidance way that catches code-level security issues such as injection and exposed secrets during the implementation phase.
softwaredev/environment/container-safety: Container definition as developer-safety surface
Container definitions (Dockerfiles, Compose, devcontainers) are treated as a safety surface for the developer's own machine, not just a build recipe.
Least privilege in container definitions
Grant builds the minimum privilege: no privileged mode, drop unneeded capabilities, and don't mount the docker socket.
Match container uid/gid to host user
Align container user IDs with the host user, or run with the host identity, so artifacts are owned by the developer.
Multi-stage builds with slim non-root runtime
Build in one stage and copy artifacts into a slim non-root runtime stage, keeping root and build tooling out of the final image.
Narrow read-only mounts
Mount the narrowest path possible, read-only where feasible, and never mount broad paths like home or the root filesystem into a build.
Root-by-default blast radius
Running container builds as root by default widens the damage that ordinary mistakes can cause on the host, especially via bind mounts.
Root-owned artifacts on bind mounts
Builds running as root write root-owned files into bind-mounted host paths, which then require elevated privilege to clean up.
Run as host identity for throwaway builds
For throwaway local builds, skip the in-image user and run as the host user so artifacts are owned by you and need no elevated cleanup.
Run as non-root user
Set a non-root user for the build/run stage so root in the container is not root on host bind mounts.
Swiss cheese model
A framing in which multiple layers of defense each have holes, and harm occurs when the holes align; here, muscle-memory cleanup commands landing on the wrong target.
softwaredev/environment/debugging: Check recent changes
Review recent commits and diffs to identify changes that may have introduced the bug.
Check the obvious causes
Check common simple causes: typos, wrong file, stale cache, wrong branch, missing environment variable.
Debugging way
Child way covering systematic debugging.
Find the introducing commit by bisecting
When stuck, use version control tools (such as git bisect) to find the commit that introduced the bug.
One change, one test
Fix only one thing at a time so each change can be tested individually.
Read full error message and stack trace
Before modifying code, thoroughly read the complete error message and stack trace to understand the failure.
Reproduce the issue before fixing
Trigger the issue yourself before attempting a fix, because a fix cannot be verified if the failure cannot be reproduced.
Search codebase for error string
Locate the origin of a failure by searching the codebase for the literal error text.
Targeted logging at function boundaries
Add logging at function boundaries rather than scattering it throughout the code.
Trace back to the source
The bug is not necessarily where the error appears; trace backward to find its true source.
Verify root cause before changing code
Do not change code based on guesses; confirm the root cause first.
softwaredev/environment/deps: Avoid trivial packages
Guidance not to add packages for trivial functionality.
Dependency security practices
Scan dependencies after adding or updating, address vulnerability warnings by fixing or documenting exceptions, and flag dependencies more than 2 major versions behind.
Dependency update practices
Practices when updating dependencies: read changelog for breaking changes, update one package at a time when debugging, run tests after each update.
Flag dependencies far behind on major versions
Flag dependencies that are more than 2 major versions behind the current release.
Maintenance check
Assessing whether a package is maintained by examining last publish date and open issues.
Necessity check (write it in <50 lines)
Evaluate whether a dependency is really needed by considering whether the functionality could be written in fewer than 50 lines.
Package size and license check
Checking a package's size and license before adopting it.
Pre-dependency evaluation checklist
A set of questions to ask before adding a dependency, covering necessity, maintenance, size, license, triviality, and wrapper status.
Run tests after each update
Running the test suite after every dependency update to catch regressions.
Wrapper package check
Reading a package's manifest to see if one dependency does the real work, then comparing adoption and considering taking that dependency directly.
code/supplychain/depscan way
A referenced way on automated vulnerability scanning of dependencies.
code/supplychain/maturity way
A referenced way on software supply chain maturity for dependency evaluation.
softwaredev/environment/hostparity: Authoring host evidence is only about the authoring host
A green result on the authoring machine is evidence only about that machine; claims about the target must come from the target.
Categories where hosts differ and cause divergent behavior: OS and shell, tool versions, env vars and secrets, file case sensitivity, network access, working directory, clock and locale.
Common excuses for skipping target validation, such as 'It's the same code', 'CI will catch it', 'I ran the tests', 'The file is right there', each with a counter.
Reports must name hosts, stating 'Verified on the authoring host only; unverified on <target>' once per target and citing how a target was exercised (CI run URL, image tag).
A local model, service, or credential standing in for a remote one serves iteration but the remote supplies the evidence.
Run target locally via matching container
When the target can be run locally (e.g., GitHub Actions, a container matching the runner, same base image), run it there before claiming parity.
Rule that a file resolved from the working tree but untracked, ignored, or unpushed does not exist for CI, teammates, or the deployed artifact.
Validate where it runs, or say that you did not
Rule that a change must be exercised on the target host (CI runner, container, staging, other OS), or each unreachable target must be named as unverified.
softwaredev/environment/makefile: CI parity
CI should run the same Make targets as humans so the commands live in one place.
Composable targets
Make targets chain together so CI and humans run the same commands.
Discoverable targets
Makefile targets can be listed and read to reveal what is available and how it works.
Don't duplicate commands
If an existing command works, the Make target should call it rather than reimplement it.
Keep recipes short
A target should be 1-3 commands; complex logic belongs in a script that Make calls.
Language-agnostic wrapper
Make wraps npm, cargo, pip, go, or any other tool without replacing them.
Make zero dependencies
Make is installed on every Unix system and available on Windows via WSL/MSYS, requiring no extra installation.
Makefile as task runner
A Makefile serves as a project's task runner, answering how to build, test, or lint the repo regardless of language or toolchain.
Read Makefile before writing
If a Makefile exists, run help or read it before adding targets or inventing ad-hoc commands.
Scaffold Makefile early in new repos
For a new repo, scaffold a Makefile early as the project's control panel; for existing repos without one, propose one when build/test commands are scattered.
Self-documenting help
A pattern where each target documents itself via comments so a help target can list targets with descriptions.
Standard Makefile targets
Conventional target names such as help, install, build, test, lint, fmt, clean, docs, release, dist, and check that projects should prefer, though not all are required.
Use variables for tunables
Versions, paths, and flags should be defined as variables at the top of the Makefile.
softwaredev/environment/recovery: Ambiguity failure
A failure where the worker asked a question, guessed, or artifacts contradict each other; fix the cheapest upstream artifact owning the confusion and re-delegate.
Capability failure
A failure where the instrument is wrong for the job (wrong specialist, missing expertise, out-of-domain handback); the move is to change agent, tool, or approach.
Classify failure before reacting
Principle that a failed attempt must be classified into a failure class before choosing a recovery move, rather than reflexively retrying, re-briefing, or adding context.
Clock agreement check for timing diagnosis
Before trusting timing comparisons across two processes, confirm clocks agree via a log line carrying both processes' timestamps and anchor conclusions to absolute timestamps.
Deterministic failure
A failure where the same input reproduces the same failure, such as compile errors, failing assertions, lint, or schema rejection; requires changing the input before re-running.
Gate red twice
A gate failing twice on the same increment signals the increment is wrong-sized or the plan is wrong; split or rescope and return through a failing test.
Intermittent defect mechanism-level verification

Intermittent failures are confirmed fixed only with mechanism-level evidence showing the causal path is gone; a lower failure rate proves nothing, and diagnostics must be captured before exposure-reducing changes.
No-progress attempt counts as failed
An attempt yielding no new artifact, evidence, or narrowed hypothesis is a failed attempt that consumes one of the three; spinning without progress enables runaway loops.
Preserve partial work in handback
A failed attempt's evidence (failing test, authored file, exact error, classification) is carried in the handback with status, failure class, and what survives.
Reflexive retry
The reflex after failure to run the same thing again, brief the same worker harder, or feed more context, which spends a turn on the class of failure least likely to yield.
Substitutions are plan changes
Substituting a weaker gate, smaller scope, or different agent is a plan change to be recorded where the plan lives with the prompting failure; successful recoveries are recorded too.
Systemic failure
A failure of the harness itself, such as a wedged delegation, missing tool, broken gate infrastructure, or hard cap; stop and report to the operator with exact evidence.
Three attempts then escalate
A unit of work gets three attempts across all strategies combined; the fourth move is escalation to the operator with class history and evidence.
Transient failure
An environment flake such as network, rate limit, race, or resource exhaustion; allowed move is an unchanged retry, max 2, with backoff.
softwaredev/environment/ssh: Assume intentional access
Assume the user has configured SSH access intentionally, and if connection fails, ask before troubleshooting rather than assuming setup is broken.
BatchMode
An SSH option that makes the connection fail immediately if authentication needs interaction, preventing hangs on unexpected prompts.
ConnectTimeout
An SSH option that bounds connection time so commands do not hang on unreachable hosts or network issues.
Dev / personal SSH environment
Environments where keys are in the standard location and ssh-agent is running, allowing straightforward SSH use.
Enterprise / legacy SSH environment
Environments that may require password-based authentication via sshpass.
Hardcoding passwords in commands
Embedding passwords directly in commands, which is prohibited.
Homelab / internal SSH environment
Environments with multiple hosts and possibly jump hosts, handled using SSH config.
Interactive password entry
Attempting to type passwords into interactive prompts, which Claude cannot do and which causes hangs.
Key-based authentication
Authentication using SSH keys rather than passwords, preferred over password auth.
Non-interactive SSH commands
SSH invocations must not require interactive input, since Claude cannot respond to password prompts and interactive commands hang indefinitely.
StrictHostKeyChecking accept-new
An SSH option that accepts new hosts but rejects changed host keys.
Suggest SSH setup when missing
When the user wants SSH but it is not configured, suggest setup steps and then retest the connection.
sshpass cautions
Guidelines for sshpass: password is visible in environment, prefer key-based auth, and source passwords from env var or file, never hardcode.
softwaredev/freshness: Artifacts derived from a source (README from code, lockfile from manifest, generated client from schema) can fall behind silently without failing.
The way covers consistency drift, not available upgrades; newer dependency versions belong to code/supplychain/depscan.
The check reads history, so it detects abandoned artifacts but misses artifacts still edited yet factually wrong, such as stale counts, dead links, or mismatched lists.
A note is a prompt for judgment rather than a mandate; a stable utility's year-old README is often still right.
A parked ADR calls for one of three moves: accept it, reject it, or document what it is waiting on.
A note triggered when ADRs remain in Draft or Proposed status past an age threshold.
When in a flagged file, verify the parts asserting facts against the current source.
A note triggered when documentation's git history lags HEAD by many commits with no branch carrying an update.
softwaredev/freshness/groundtruth: When drift is pervasive, write one fresh baseline describing the implemented system and supersede drifted predecessor docs while preserving them as history.
A citation, attribution, or named term in one's own output is itself a claim and must be verified against the cited artifact rather than memory.
Derive ground truth from executable artifacts
Practice of determining actual system behavior from running code, schema/migrations, and runtime-read config rather than prose.
A doc/code gap should be surfaced and classified as doc stale, code wrong, or both adrift, with evidence.
After a change, the gate passes when output matches baseline except an enumerated list of deliberate deltas; unexplained diffs must be justified and baselines never silently re-baselined.
Capturing current observable outputs over representative inputs, normalized for volatile leaves, before a refactor or migration, to diff against afterward.
Treating ADRs, design notes, specs, READMEs, and docstrings as claims that must be confirmed against executable artifacts before reliance.
A document that is still read, edited, and trusted but is semantically wrong relative to what the code implements; not detectable by history age.
A wrong premise adopted early mis-shapes everything built on it, so measurements taken against a stale model are all off.
softwaredev/tooling: Renaming an ADR involves editing heading, moving the file, and refreshing an index; a tool command owns all three steps atomically.
Build the tool, don't repeat the incantation
Principle that repeated, error-prone, or rule-encoding operations should be made into tool commands rather than manual shell sequences.
The criterion for building a tool is repetition multiplied by risk, not novelty; one-off operations don't merit tooling.
The payoff of encoding operations into tools: typed, validated, lint-enforced procedures cost one command instead of minutes of careful manual effort.
Signals that an operation should become a subcommand: multi-step sequences, encoded conventions, repetition, and care-requiring reversible steps.
Conventions such as numbering, naming, and file layout should be owned by the tool rather than by documentation humans follow by hand.
A tool subcommand is discoverable, testable, and self-documenting, unlike a remembered incantation which rots when its knower leaves.
softwaredev/visualization: Bar, line, and histogram charts used to display quantitative data, rendered from piped JSON.
Diagram types suited to showing relationships between entities.
A text-based diagram syntax used for structural diagrams.
The guidance is a soft suggestion to use visuals when appropriate, not a required rule.
Diagram types suited to walkthroughs of sequential processes.
A table mapping types of user requests (e.g., 'Walk me through', 'How does X work?') to suitable visual forms such as sequence diagrams, flowcharts, charts, ER diagrams, or tables.
Rendering diagrams and charts directly to the terminal using tools provided in the children of this way.
A guideline to consider using a diagram instead of prose when explaining structural things such as workflows, lifecycles, or component interactions.
softwaredev/visualization/charts: Chart type selection by purpose
Choosing the chart type that fits the task: quick trend, category comparison, time series, distribution, or compact summary.
Chart types
The set of chart formats supported by the tool, including spark, bar, hbar, line, table and hist, each suited to a particular data-display purpose.
Distribution of raw values
The spread of raw values, displayed with the hist chart.
JSON stdin input
Chart data is supplied as JSON piped through standard input, with optional fields having sensible defaults.
K/M suffix number formatting
A formatting option that abbreviates numbers with K and M suffixes, versus the default of using commas.
Label-to-value map input
Input form mapping labels to values, used for bar, hbar and table charts (table also accepts string values).
Number array input
Input form consisting of an array of numbers, used for spark, line and hist charts.
Time series and trends
Data over time, best displayed with the line chart using braille rendering.
Visualize instead of printing raw numbers
Guidance that when asked to visualize data, show trends, compare values or display metrics, a chart should be rendered rather than raw numbers printed.
chart-tool
A tool that renders ANSI terminal charts from JSON piped to it via stdin.
softwaredev/visualization/diagrams: Choose the right diagram type
Matching the content (sequences, states, decisions, relationships, timelines, git) to the appropriate Mermaid diagram type rather than defaulting to flowchart.
Flowchart overuse mistake
The common mistake of using flowchart for all content, even when it has a time axis or state transitions.
GitHub Mermaid compatibility
Handling GitHub's Mermaid renderer quirks, such as line breaks in node labels, escaping angle brackets, and avoiding brackets in sequence messages.
Stdin piping usage
Mermaid syntax can be piped to mmaid via stdin, or a file can be rendered directly.
mmaid
A command-line tool that renders Mermaid diagram syntax as diagrams in the terminal, with Unicode or ASCII output.
mmaid discovery resolution order
The ordered lookup for the mmaid binary: system PATH first, then XDG cache, then suggesting installation if not found.
mmaid flags
Command-line options controlling theme, ASCII-only output, fenced code block wrapping, file insertion, padding, sharp corners, and sample output.
mmaid installation options
Ways to install mmaid when absent: Arch Linux AUR, Go install, or direct download.
mmaid themes
Color themes for mmaid output, some with solid backgrounds that support depth-based region coloring in subgraphs.
mmaid vs chart-tool
Guidance that mmaid is for structural diagrams while chart-tool is for quantitative data visualization.
workstation/pkghistory: Age as weak signal
Install date is a poor indicator of whether a package is unneeded, since stable tools may go untouched yet remain in use.
Builder layer
Packages the user authored themselves (own AUR/local builds), marking needs that no existing tool fit.
Burst signature
Several related packages installed on the same day, indicating one focused sitting with a goal.
Cull before persisting inventory
Do not record a curated inventory before the cull, since documenting soon-to-be-removed cruft wastes effort; record post-cull state instead.
Deliberate adds extraction
Focusing first on deliberately installed packages (AUR/manual/explicit) across package managers rather than native repo base noise.
Install is not use
A limitation: the log shows intent to install but has no telemetry on what actually runs.
Mermaid timeline rendering
Showing sequential phases over time as a Mermaid diagram rendered for terminal art instead of narrating.
Orphan signature
A cluster of packages that appeared once and never recruited neighbors or was revisited; the strong cull signal.
Package history as behavioral journal
The idea that a package manager's log is an involuntary, timestamped record of user intent that should be read as a time series.
Recruitment as cull signal
The principle that whether a theme continues to attract new packages is a stronger indicator of abandonment than install age.
Redundancy clusters
Overlapping packages within a subject group, such as two remote-desktop stacks or multiple themes, where cull candidates hide.
Reverse-dependency check before removal
Verifying reverse dependencies via a dry run before removing packages, with the user driving every removal.
Survivorship limitation
Current-state package listings show only surviving packages, omitting removals and upgrade churn; the transaction log gives the true series.
Thread signature
A theme recurring across months in the package log, indicating durable interest or identity.
workstation/shell: Ask before installing
Principle of confirming user preferences (font, CLI replacements, git identity, SSH key type) before running package manager commands.
Detect first, install second
Principle of identifying the OS and package manager before recommending install commands, since package names differ across distros.
Global git config
The user-level git identity and preferences file, set once per machine and inherited by every repo unless overridden locally.
Graceful degradation
Principle that every sourced config checks for a tool before configuring it, so a missing tool silently no-ops.
Layer on top, don't clobber
Principle of adding to existing PATH and XDG defaults set by distros and Homebrew rather than replacing them.
Modern CLI tools
Modern replacement command-line tools such as lsd, bat, fd, rg, and fzf.
Modular shellrc, PATH, XDG
Organizing shell configuration into modular sourced files along with PATH and XDG settings.
No plugin managers by default
Principle of preferring plain shell and sourced files over plugin managers like oh-my-zsh, zinit, or antibody unless the user asks.
Package manager
System-specific software installers: Homebrew on macOS, pacman on Arch, apt on Debian/Ubuntu, dnf on Fedora.
Persistent ssh-agent
A locally set up ssh-agent that persists, one of the shell setup concerns; distinct from non-interactive SSH use from Claude.
Project-level configuration
Configuration that lives at the project level, distinct from workstation shell setup.
Walkthrough shape
Interactive setup structured as a sequence of detect, confirm, install, verify, reporting findings and awaiting confirmation at each step rather than batch-installing.
Workstation Shell
The shell layer of a personal developer machine, covering what a user cares about on a fresh install, separate from project-level config.
workstation/shell/gitconfig: Conventions for commit messages that build on top of the configured git identity.
A git config feature for using different identities (e.g., personal vs work), to be set up only when the user confirms the split.
Delta is a git pager configured in the global config, installed via workstation shell tools.
The user-level git identity and preferences file, set once per machine and inherited by every repo unless overridden locally.
A global excludes file (~/.gitignore_global) for noise never relevant anywhere, distinct from per-project ignores.
A git credential helper chosen according to the operating system (macOS, Linux GNOME, Linux generic, Windows) for HTTPS authentication.
Project-specific ignore rules kept in each project's own .gitignore rather than the global file.
Push via SSH uses keys held in ssh-agent, so no credential helper is needed.
workstation/shell/shell-prompt: Symptom where a freshly installed prompt theme shows boxes because the terminal uses a plain font or the prompt engine is misconfigured.
The font is installed at OS level and then selected in the terminal emulator's settings; the shell cannot set it.
A shell prompt (oh-my-posh, starship, powerlevel10k) that renders branch, git status, and system icons using glyphs.
A patched font containing extra icon glyphs required for glyph-rich prompts to display icons.
Nerd font installation via package manager
Installing nerd fonts using brew, pacman, apt, or dnf, with apt lacking a first-class package.
The component running in the shell that emits escape sequences referencing glyphs by codepoint.
Theme files that ship with the prompt binary; if a named theme is missing they can be fetched remotely after asking the user.
Restart terminal and remind user of GUI step
After font install, the terminal must be restarted and its font changed manually; the agent should tell the user what to look for and which font to pick.
The GUI application (alacritty, kitty, wezterm, iTerm2, GNOME Terminal, Windows Terminal) that renders text and holds font settings.
workstation/shell/shellrc: Disable-by-rename
Fragments can be selectively disabled by renaming them so they are no longer sourced.
Fragment header comment
Each config fragment file begins with a one-line comment stating its purpose.
Graceful degradation
Principle that every sourced config checks for a tool before configuring it, so a missing tool silently no-ops.
Lexicographic filename ordering contract
Config fragments are loaded in lexicographic order by filename, using numeric prefixes to define load order.
Modern CLI tools
Modern replacement command-line tools such as lsd, bat, fd, rg, and fzf.
Prepend user paths, keep distro defaults tail
PATH composition places user paths first while keeping distro defaults at the end, with deduplication to keep entries unique.
Respect existing OS/login manager settings
A pattern that respects variables the OS or login manager already set rather than overriding them.
SSH agent
SSH agent is loaded by a dedicated fragment (04-ssh.zsh).
Silent no-op on missing tools
Each fragment guards against missing tools and silently does nothing rather than raising errors.
Suggested fragment layout
A table of numbered fragment files covering XDG, PATH, env, package hooks, SSH agent, Go, Node, aliases, completion, and prompt init.
Thin rc file sourcing fragments
A minimal shell rc file that sources individual config fragments from a directory such as conf.d, instead of a monolithic rc file.
Workstation Shell
The shell layer of a personal developer machine, covering what a user cares about on a fresh install, separate from project-level config.
oh-my-posh prompt
oh-my-posh is a prompt engine initialized by a shell fragment (09-omp.zsh).
workstation/shell/sshagent: The message 'The agent has no identities' means the socket is live but keys are not loaded, requiring ssh-add.
Launching a fresh ssh-agent in every new shell results in multiple agents that do not have the user's keys loaded.
On Linux the agent must be managed so only one runs per user session, via a socket pattern, systemd user service, or desktop keyring.
Using SSH non-interactively with BatchMode, ConnectTimeout, and remote command execution, covered separately from local agent management.
If the desktop session (gnome-keyring or KWallet) already runs an agent, use it and check before spawning another.
SSH silently refuses to use keys if file permissions are wrong.
Generating a key with ssh-keygen using the Ed25519 algorithm, which is smaller, faster and stronger than RSA, with an optional passphrase.
Using a fixed, well-known socket path that the first shell creates and subsequent shells reuse, giving one persistent agent per user session.
macOS ships an ssh-agent that launchd starts on demand, with passphrases stored in Keychain to survive reboot.
workstation/shell/tools: Ask before aliasing
Practice of asking the user before aliasing new tools over original POSIX command names, since some users want originals untouched.
Bat extras
Optional bat companion tools that should be mentioned to the user and installed only after asking.
Debian/Ubuntu name collision symlink
On Debian/Ubuntu, fd and bat install under alternate names to avoid collisions; create a symlink or alias to the expected name in the conf.d include.
Package name drift
Package and binary names for the same tool differ across package managers (brew, pacman, apt, dnf), notably fd and bat on Debian/Ubuntu.
Shell config in conf.d includes
Aliases, MANPAGER, completions and key-binding scripts live in sourced conf.d includes rather than the main rc file.
Sixel image support
Inline terminal images only render in sixel-capable terminals, so terminal capability should be checked before installing.
bat as man pager (MANPAGER)
Configuring MANPAGER to pipe through bat for colored man pages, with a batman function wrapper.
fzf shell integration
fzf provides ctrl-r, ctrl-t and alt-c key bindings through shell-integration scripts whose path differs by installer.
gh interactive auth
After installing gh, the user is prompted to run the auth login themselves; the agent should not drive the interactive OAuth flow.
lsd vs eza choice
Both lsd and eza are active ls replacements; eza is the maintained fork of exa while lsd has more glyph-heavy defaults, so the user should be asked which to use.
zoxide smart cd
zoxide provides smart directory jumping and overrides cd via its init integration.
writing: Ask user about style
Elicit voice, tone and register preferences early using precise literary terms rather than assuming.
Code documentation
Documentation such as README, docstrings and API docs, handled by the Docs Way rather than this guidance.
Default prose style rules
Overridable defaults: active voice, no staccato fragments, conclusion-first or context-first by audience, cutting filler, naming real terms with a gloss.
General content creation scope
Writing guidance covering proposals, reports, presentations, memos and briefs, distinct from code documentation.
Genre-specific priorities
Each genre (technical doc, ADR, agent brief, proposal, status update) has its own priorities and pitfalls, and takes precedence over general style rules where they conflict.
Outline before drafting
Practice of outlining a document's structure and defending it to the user before writing the draft.
Pre-writing checklist
Questions to settle before drafting: audience, format, core message, and style.
Prose anti-patterns
Patterns to avoid: corporate filler, constructivism framing (it's not X, it's Y), and adjective stacking.
Prose over bullet points
Style principle favoring developed prose with varied sentence rhythm over bullet lists disguised as prose.
Pushback on mismatched format
When the requested format doesn't suit the content, explain why and suggest an alternative while preserving the user's intent.
Revision in passes
Revising sequentially for structure, clarity, tone, and concision rather than all at once.
